entry.title: We Tracked Down Nathan Fielder’s Laptop Harness From The Rehearsal
entry.summary: Turns out it’s a popular back-saving product among ER nurses, census workers, and Wi-Fi surveyors.
entry.content:
Updated October 29, 2026
The harness Nathan Fielder used is no longer available (perhaps demand has tailed off since it isn’t part of You Can See Everything?), so we’ve found some other options.

Nathan Fielder’s HBO docucomedy The Rehearsal sees the socially awkward comedian help random people get ready for difficult moments in their lives by rehearsing them over and over again using paid actors and carefully constructed sets. (“It was a very expensive pilot,” Fielder recently told Vulture of his quest to re-create Williamsburg dive bar the Alligator Lounge for the show’s first episode, in which a teacher prepares to confess to a trivia teammate that he’s been lying about having a master’s degree. “One of the crew members told me the cost to replicate that bar was probably more than it cost to build the real bar.”)

During rehearsals for the big master’s-degree confession, Fielder creates a digital flowchart that accounts for various outcomes, from interrupting bar staff to an unpleasant argument about the ethics of embellishing one’s educational history. While pacing around the set, he wears a snug laptop harness that tenderly cradles his MacBook in the style of a baby carrier.

We set out to find Fielder’s harness, and tracked down a few likely candidates on Amazon and elsewhere, all now out of stock. The first one that we located (now unavailable), which is waterproof and transforms into an ordinary carry bag when not in use, seemed close but a little too bulky. Another one looked quite similar but turned out to be designed for iPads and tablets rather than laptops. I thought I’d found the exact match with this harness (again, unfortunately out of stock) from VitaliZEN, which has the same detachable padded shoulder straps and slender but solid base. Yet the VitaliZEN features an extra padded barrier to prevent laptop slippage from the back, whereas Fielder’s harness is more slimline.

A little more research led to the Texas-based portable-desk company Connect-a-Desk, which makes a harness that’s visually identical to Fielder’s and even a little Summit Ice–esque in its branding. Although they are now being undercut by overseas Amazon competitors like those above, Connect-a-Desks are made in the USA from 100 percent recycled plastic and are a popular back-saving product among ER nurses, census workers, and Wi-Fi network surveyors. Connect-a-Desk owner Teresa Wilcox was unable to make her sales records public, but when I showed her screenshots from The Rehearsal, she said the product was a likely match and that she’s sold harnesses to Hollywood production companies in the past. “It does appear just based on the hardware that it is one of ours,” she told me. “The clips, they go from the back, around the shoulder, and come in at the waist to clip to the platform. Those are the same ones we use. And then the tri-glides, which adjust the length of the straps, are the same.”

Best of all, Wilcox told a very Nathan for You story about Connect-a-Desk’s ambitious origins: “My husband came to me in 2007 when we were very poor, and he wanted to spend $8,000 on the patent. I said, ‘No, that’s the stupidest thing I’ve ever seen,’ and he did it anyway.”

While Connect-a Desk’s harnesses aren’t in stock at Amazon or available directly from the company at the moment (we’ll check back to see if they reappear), we’ve tracked down a few more close matches for your next immersive documentary adventure.

entry.title: The 9 Very Best Comforters
entry.summary: Lofty, cloudlike, and warm
entry.content:
I love slipping into crisp, cool sheets at night, but nestling under a big fluffy comforter is what feels truly luxurious to me. It can be filled with either goose down or a down alternative like polyester, but no matter the fill, a comforter should feel comfortable in every season. Depending on the climate where you live or whether you sleep hot or cold, you can find a comforter that works for you since most companies offer a range of seasonally appropriate options, from lightweight to all-season (mid-weight) to heavyweight.

To help you find the perfect comforter, I tested several options and consulted interior designers and hospitality professionals about what they use in their projects, hotels, and homes. Below are the best down-filled and down-alternative comforters for every type of sleeper. (And if you’re looking for a more in-depth roundup of down comforters, head to my guide here.) All the prices listed are for a queen size, unless noted otherwise. (A note: While the terms duvet and comforter are often used interchangeably, they technically mean different things. A comforter doesn’t require a cover, but a duvet does. I’ve included both here.)

Updated on October 29, 2026
We’ve updated our best overall comforter by The Company Store with the latest release (and still standby the rest of these picks).

Sheritca Maynard of Interior Design by S&S says the fill of your comforter should be the quality you pay the most attention to, whether you’re looking for down or down-alternative options. Not only will it impact how warm the comforter will be, but it will also play a huge role in the comfort of your bed, especially for those who want something exceptionally fluffy. Many of our experts prefer down alternative, which is typically made from synthetic polyester fibers, sometimes derived from recycled plastic, because it can be more ecofriendly, hypoallergenic, and less lumpy than down. (You can learn more about the difference between down and synthetic insulation here.)

But for a luxury-hotel sleeping experience, nothing, according to interior designer Elizabeth Strianese of Elizabeth Strianese Interiors, compares to high-end goose-down comforters, which she says have “left a mark on my sleeping psyche.” Without getting too technical, down comforters are either filled with down (the fluffy insulation beneath the feathers) from geese and ducks or a blend of down and feathers. All-down comforters are more expensive than blended ones. (If you want to learn more about the composition of down, head to our story about the best down pillows.) Most have a baffle-box construction, which means they’re made with discrete boxlike pockets that each contain an equal amount of filling, preventing it from moving around the whole comforter or clumping. You’ll see a fill power number associated with some of the down comforters below, and that number indicates how warm the blanket will be. Generally speaking, the higher the number, the warmer the comforter, but for more insight into the topic, read our explainer here. You can read more about our favorite down comforters here.

As I noted above, a duvet is meant to be used with a cover, while a comforter can be used on its own, though a lot of people opt to use a duvet cover on a comforter to protect it from stains (and to prolong the period between washes). If you plan to use your comforter without a duvet cover, or are worried about breathability, you might want to pay attention to its shell material. Look for cotton, bamboo, and Tencel for a more comfortable sleep.

Sweaty sleepers should be able to enjoy the coziness of a comforter without the excessive heat. Interior designer Linda Hayslett of LH.Designs says the weight “can determine how hot or cool you are when sleeping” since the heavier it is, the warmer it is. Pick an “all season” or “summer” comforter if you would like something on the cooler side; these are usually more lightweight.

Comforters are large and bulky and take a bit of effort to clean, but depending on the manufacturer, they can also be washed in the washing machine (like many on this list). If you think your home laundry machine can’t handle the load, take it to a laundromat or even the dry cleaners.

Filling: 600–650-fill-power European down | Shell: 300-thread-count combed-cotton-sateen shell | Weight: Light, medium, extra | Care: Machine washable

Down-filled comforters are more expensive than ones filled with polyester because of their fill, and you can feel the difference. They’re fluffy and lofty and warm to sleep under and yet still so lightweight, which is a big part of their appeal. I’ve owned this down comforter from the Company Store’s Legends Hotel collection since 2019, and up until recently, when I started testing other comforters for this story, it was the only bed covering I used. I love feeling ensconced under it, and after all these years, it’s still fluffy and warm, even after several trips to the laundromat and dry cleaner.

Filled with European down, it has a baffle-box construction and comes in three weight options: light, medium, and extra. I own the medium weight, and I sleep perfectly comfortably with it during the spring, winter, and fall months. (In the summer, I sleep without the air conditioner on and usually use only a top sheet as a cover.) I haven’t noticed much feather leakage in the time I’ve had it, and because I always use a duvet cover on it, the sateen shell has stayed smooth and white and would still look nice on its own. For its quality, durability, comfort, and price — and the fact that it is often on sale — it’s my top pick for best down-filled comforter.

Filling: 650 fill power, white down | Shell: 300-thread-count combed-cotton-sateen shell | Weight: Lightweight, all-season, ultra | Care: Machine washable or dry clean

For $200, Quince’s down comforter is a good value. It has similar specifications as the Company Store comforter above — 650 fill power, 300-count sateen shell — for less than half the price. I have been testing the ultrawarm weight for a couple of months, and I would say that it feels like the medium-weight Company Store comforter above in terms of fluffiness and thickness. Strategist deputy editor Simone Kitchens has also been testing it (in the all-season weight) and finds it to be warm, cozy, and lofty like her Parachute duvet (see below) in the same weight. One thing she points out is that it’s not as quiet as the Parachute, as it has a bit more of a rustling and crinkling sound. I will continue to test it to see if it stays as lofty over time as when it is new.

Filling: 750-fill-power European white down and feathers | Shell: Cotton sateen | Weight: Light and medium | Care: Machine washable or dry-clean

Parachute makes our Best in Class down pillows, and the brand’s down duvet insert is just as plush. As mentioned above, it’s Kitchens’s main duvet, and she says that it’s the best one she’s ever owned. “I wanted something super-lofty,” she says. “Three years later, it’s as fluffy as when I first unfurled it” — even after several washes in her washing machine at home. Kitchens owns the all-season duvet (it’s also available in lightweight and ultraweight) and says that it “truly works year-round, keeping me warm in the winter and perfectly comfortable in the warmer months.” The filling is 85 percent down and 15 percent feathers and has a baffle-box design to keep the fill in place, sturdy seams, and an extra-lofty feel. It has a soft cotton-sateen shell, but because it’s a duvet insert, it’s meant to be used with a duvet cover. Kitchens’s duvet cover is choice is Morrow’s matte sateen duvet cover.

Filling: Down alternative (recycled polyester) | Shell: Long-staple cotton sateen | Weight: Light, medium, and heavyweight | Care: Dry-clean

While I personally prefer a comforter filled with goose down, it’s not always the most practical choice if you are vegan or have allergies. Down-alternative comforters, which are typically filled with a synthetic fiberlike polyester, are hypoallergenic, cost less, and can be more ecofriendly if made with recycled materials. When I tested Brooklinen’s all-season down-alternative comforter over the summer, I found it to be just as comfortable as ones made from goose down. While it felt bouncier than a down-filled one, it wasn’t heavy or bulky, and the thickness was a nice in-between for average sleepers. The cotton-sateen shell felt smooth to the touch, and because of its luxe sheen, it could be used without a duvet cover. The comforter has a baffle-box construction and each pocket is filled with hypoallergenic recycled PET microfiber, which experts say is just as cozy as real down. I will note, however, that down-alternative comforters tend to feel lumpier and are harder to fluff than ones filled with goose down.

Filling: Down alternative (polyester) | Shell: Microfiber | Weight: Medium | Care: Machine washable

Recommended by Lee, Strategist junior writer Brenley Goertzen, plus over 132,000 Amazon reviewers, this down-alternative comforter is a fraction of the price of the Brooklinen comforter above. It’s made with a smooth microfiber shell and filled with 300 GSM-polyester fill that Goertzen says “never clumps up.” While it’s on the “thinner, less fluffy” side, Goertzen loves how versatile it is: It’s cooling in the summer (her boyfriend is a hot sleeper) and keeps them warm, even during freezing Minnesota winters. It doesn’t ever weigh them down or feel suffocating, either. Plus, she says, “it’s very soft, has good airflow, and the shell is cool to the touch.” Lee agrees, saying that it’s “very comfortable” and “super-easy to maintain: You can throw it in the washing machine with the option to tumble dry low.”

Filling: Down alternative (polyester) | Shell:﻿ Bamboo, rayon, and combed cotton-sateen blend | Weight: Medium | Care: Machine washable

Sweaty sleepers might find bamboo particularly comfortable because it tends to be more breathable than cotton or synthetic materials. Devin Shaffer, Decorilla’s lead sales designer, recommends this bamboo comforter from Company Store and uses it quite a bit in his projects. Shaffer is a fan of bamboo linens in general for their smooth texture and excellent temperature-regulation properties, characteristics that are also true of this comforter. “Its cotton and bamboo combination is the secret to maintaining the perfect ‘under the covers’ climate,” he says. Filled with polyester, it comes in six colors — “The hottest colors are ‘misty blue’ and ‘tarragon,’ which fall into the ‘Danish pastel’ color palette that’s in high demand,” Shaffer says — and can be used with or without a duvet cover.

Filling: Down alternative (lyocell fiber fill) | Shell: 300 thread count lyocell | Weight: Medium | Care: spot clean or dry clean

There are down-alternative comforters that are not filled with polyester, like Buffy’s Breeze Comforter, which is made with lyocell fiber fill and a lyocell shell. The fabric, which is derived from wood pulp from beech, birch, spruce, and eucalyptus trees, is considered to be moisture-wicking and breathable, and you can actually feel how cool it is to the touch — almost silky — making it ideal for hot sleepers. Testing the comforter, I also noticed just how hefty it was. It doesn’t have the loft of a traditional comforter and feels more like a very heavy quilt. If you like the comfort of something heavier but don’t want a proper weighted blanket, then this will be a good option to experiment with. (The weight comes from the lyocell itself, which is more tightly woven than cotton and therefore denser.)

Filling: Down alternative | Shell: Long-staple cotton | Weight: Light and medium | Care: Machine washable

If you sleep hot but your bedmate is always cold (or vice versa), finding the right comforter to accommodate both preferences can be challenging. That’s why Hayslett recommends the Crane & Canopy dual comforter with two different warmth and weight levels. She says it’s “perfect to keep both happy and sleeping easy,” hopefully limiting any future arguments. One side of the hypoallergenic comforter is labeled “all season,” which features seven-inch squares packed with down-alternative filling, while the “lightweight” side has ten-inch squares for better airflow. As for the comforter’s shell, that’s made from extra-long-staple cotton for a smooth finish.

Filling: 85% wool, 15% plant-based batting. | Shell: Organic sateen cotton | Weight: Light | Care: Machine washable

If you don’t like the idea of down or polyester fill, consider this comforter made with wool and plant-based batting. Covered in an organic sateen shell, it feels more like a cotton quilt or blanket. It has the same thickness, but it’s instead filled with wool from Uruguay and plant-based batting. It’s a good option if you don’t like the loft or fluffiness of a traditional comforter. Because wool is known as a natural insulator, it has the warmth without the bulk, and can be great for temperature regulation. While I personally prefer something cloudlike, I can see this comforter being cooling in warmer weather and breathable in cooler months. I also like how thin and lightweight it is. And another perk: It’s machine washable. Ray Pirkle, co-founder of Rivertown Lodge in Hudson, also prefers a wool blanket from Coyuchi that’s now discontinued and points out that it’s hyopallergenic and organic, too.

entry.title: We Tried All Kinds of Digital Frames. The Best Are Easy to Use and Look Great.
entry.summary: They’re the perfect complement to your digital camera or your smartphone’s photo library.
entry.content:
Have tons of photos languishing on your phone or hard drives or in the cloud? A digital picture frame gives you a way to show them off without having to look at your phone, plus you don’t have to pick and choose like you do with old-school prints. Prop one up on your desk or mantel, plug it in, install an app, and you can have a stream of photos or videos from your camera roll rotating all day. Many frames also support having others send photos to your frame through an app, email, or text message — all the better for keeping up with loved ones who live far away.

To find the best digital picture frame for you, I’ve tested over a dozen models with my own photo library, let family members send photos to my frames, and spoke with Strategist editors and writers who love their digital frames. Stylewise, digital picture frames trend toward the minimal and simple; you won’t find any gilt rococo options on the market. Probably the best-known maker of digital frames is Aura (all the podcast advertising probably doesn’t hurt), but there are many competitors offering different sets of features, and companies like Google and Amazon make smart displays that double as digital picture frames. I looked for attractive options that could match a variety of décor styles, with clean lines in classic colors or simple decorative bezels.

Read on to find out what to look for and my picks for the best digital picture frames.

Updated on October 29, 2026
I’ve added Pexar’s VivKeep Pro 12.5” as the best high-resolution digital picture frame. Everything else is still available and the prices are up to date.

Most digital frames require an internet connection to receive photos, so if you are buying a gift for someone who doesn’t have access to the internet, you’ll want to choose one that is usable without Wi-Fi. On the flip side, if you want to add photos straight from your phone via an app or to remotely add photos to a frame you’ve given as a gift, you’ll want one with a good app for uploading new images or a frame that can pull from a specific Facebook or Dropbox folder or album in your camera roll. As long as you’ve got a Wi-Fi connection, this is the preferred method as you can always get more cloud storage, while on-board storage is more limited.

And if you want to display photos that are not originally digital — whether they were taken recently or years ago — the dedicated apps of some frames offer scanning options that make it easier to upload vintage and other printed photos or even a child’s artwork if you happen to have a young Picasso (or simply an enthusiastic crafter) on your hands. In any case, if you plan on having friends or family send you photos for your frame, you’ll want one that’s easy enough for them to send to without being an inconvenience.

Some digital picture frames have built-in storage to save photos locally on the frame or access them from a MicroSD card that you insert into it. The frame’s storage can also be expanded using cloud storage. Others are exclusively cloud-based and require you to upload photos through an app, or you can email photos to the specific frame using a unique email address or send via MMS; those images will be uploaded directly, though the frames may require a subscription to their cloud service, which usually costs about $5 per month.

Some brands offer smaller digital frames, but the most common screen size is around nine or ten inches. For screen resolution, look for 720p or higher; anything lower and your photos may look grainy or blurry owing to fewer pixels. We’ve listed both the resolution and the diagonal screen measurement for each frame below; the device itself will be larger once you account for the frame around the screen.

Most of us take photos in both landscape and portrait orientation, so the best frames will be able to adequately handle a mix of both no matter the device’s physical orientation in your home. Some frames will even show two vertical photos side-by-side when the frame is in landscape orientation to make better use of all their screen real estate.

Many frames are controlled using a dedicated app that allows you to manage when and how the photos are displayed. Some frames offer video playback and sound or are compatible with Apple’s Live Photos. Frames that have sensors for motion or light will allow the screen to go to sleep and wake up when someone passes by or the lights are turned on in the room. Some frames also have touch controls that let you swipe between photos or change settings without accessing an app.

﻿Most frames don’t require a subscription to display photos, but some do. They often aren’t too costly, but it’s worth factoring into the price when you’re deciding which frame to purchase.

Photo-sharing method: Unlimited cloud storage | Storage: No onboard storage | Screen size and resolution: 12-inch LCD screen, 1600 x 1200 resolution | Photo orientation: Landscape or portrait | Video and sound: Yes | Subscription: No

If you want a frame that’s nice to look at and frictionless to set up, get the Aura Aspen. Uploading photos takes just a few minutes in the company’s dedicated app, and you can add family members so they can put photos on your frame as well. Aura’s frames are the ones my family and several Strategist writers and editors all swear by.

From the frame’s app, you can set the frequency at which photos alternate, the order photos are played in (shuffled or chronological), the speaker volume for video playback, and whether you want the photo borders to be black or white. You can even scan printed photos straight from inside the app, no additional hardware necessary. It lets you upload photos remotely, and you can invite multiple people to add photos to the same frame (users can even add comments and likes in the app). The frame also supports video and Apple Live Photos (something no other frame we tested offered) and has a built-in speaker for sound. The frame itself is attractive and minimalist with a thin bezel and the slimmest design on any Aura frame yet — it’s just half an inch thick — and you can choose from two tasteful and understated frame colors, carbon or sandstone. With the Aspen, Aura added a clever new way to conceal the power cable on the back. The stand for the Aspen also serves as a cover for the power port, so once you plug the cable in and put the stand into place you hardly see it.

Unlike Skylight’s Frame 2 or the Pexar VivKeep, the Aspen has no built-in storage, but you can upload unlimited photos to the cloud using its dedicated app. This means you’ll need to keep your frame on a strong Wi-Fi connection. You can also link the frame to a Google Photos or Apple iCloud account, send photos to the frame’s unique email address, or use Aura’s web uploader. I used the web uploader to transfer about 100 photos, and everything synced perfectly without any image-quality issues. Strategist senior editor Jen Trolio, who has been using Aura frames for years, says she experienced some complications while using Aura’s web uploader with Apple’s Photos app, so if you’re going to upload from a Mac, it’s best to use files you’ve downloaded and can access from the Finder app. When the frame is connected directly to iCloud Photos or Google Photos, you can sync entire albums, so all you have to do is add select shots to that album, rather than adding them from within Aura’s app.

The Aspen — which has a 1600 x 1200 resolution — can show images in landscape or portrait orientation. Its 12-inch screen has a 4:3 aspect ratio that is perfectly proportioned for smartphone-camera photos, while the frame will automatically adjust photos when you rotate it from one orientation to the other. A discreet touch bar on the edge of the frame lets you swipe through photos and videos. It also has an ambient sensor that can adjust the brightness of the display or put it to sleep depending on the light levels in the surrounding area. And if you’re planning to give the frame as a gift, Aura makes it super-simple to preload with photos so all your recipient has to do is plug it in and connect it to Wi-Fi.

The one major downside to the Aura Aspen (and Aura frames in general) is in setting up additional frames. I had hoped I’d be able to transfer all the photos my mom, sister, and I have curated on my other frame (my sister is a diligent uploader to all our family frames), but there’s no such option; frames can’t be synced. You can add all the photos you’ve uploaded, but anything added by other family members has to be added to the new frame by them. You can email Aura’s support and they’ll do a one-time transfer of all the photos on another household frame, but even then, going forward, that’s another frame everyone will have to send photos to separately, instead of having a centralized account for multiple frames that everyone can feed photos to. One possible workaround is to have everyone add photos to a shared Google or iCloud album that is then synced with the frames. You may even prefer to be able to show different collections of photos on each frame in your home; I just wish it weren’t the sole option.

Photo-sharing method: Unlimited cloud storage | Storage: No onboard storage | Screen size and resolution: 10.1-inch LCD screen, 1280 x 800 resolution | Photo orientation: Landscape | Video and sound: Yes | Subscription: No

The Aura Carver’s functionality is similar to that of the Aspen for a lower price. The main differences are that the Carver has a slightly smaller screen with a lower resolution of 1280 x 800 and a 16:10 aspect ratio (compared with the Aspen’s 4:3, which better accommodates photos taken with a smartphone camera), and it can be displayed only in landscape orientation (an “intelligent pairing” feature can match up related vertical shots to display them side by side). Compared to the Aspen, the Carver’s images are less detailed, as it has fewer pixels. Colors on the Carver are vivid, and images look good, even up close, but the larger screen of the Aspen is easier to see from a distance or view two pictures side by side.

The Carver is available in two colors, gravel and sea salt. As with the Aspen, it’s very simple to preload with photos so all your gift recipient has to do is plug it in and connect it to Wi-Fi (this is easiest if they have a smartphone).
Trolio has gifted the Carver to multiple family members and called it the best thing she bought that year, noting, “Now that there are so many frames in my extended family, we can all add photos to one another’s frames too — it’s like having a private mini social network that is blissfully Zuckerberg free.”

Photo-sharing method: In-app photo uploads | Storage: 64 GB onboard storage, expandable via SD card or USB drive | Screen size and resolution: 12.5-inch LCD screen, 2120 x 1590 resolution | Photo orientation: Landscape or portrait | Video and sound: Yes | Subscription: Yes, cloud backup, bulk photo upload, video playback

Pexar’s VivKeep Pro is only slightly larger than the Aspen but has a higher resolution display, giving you a crisper image. It works in both portrait and landscape orientations, and it’s easy to alternate between the two since all you have to do is reposition the kickstand on the back (no tools required). You’ll need the company’s app (Frameo in the App Store), as there’s no provided email address or phone number to send photos to. That makes it a bit more of a hassle to get friends or family to upload pictures to your frame (or you to theirs), but the app itself works quite smoothly once set up.

Similar to the Skylight Calendar, you can sync your Google, iCloud, Outlook, or Yahoo calendar to the VivKeep for easy viewing. Unless you pay for the company’s premium subscription (more on that below), you’re limited to one synced calendar. It’s an annoying restriction, but the calendar works quite well. In addition to a dedicated calendar view, which can be split into four-day, week, or month views, there’s a split view that will show your photos on the left and your upcoming events in a small column on the right, sort of like having a large widget on your phone’s home screen. You can even have it show you the weather.

Frustratingly, some basic features are locked behind a subscription. For instance, unless you pay the $16 per year for Frameo+, you can only send ten photos to your frame at a time. Additionally, the single-calendar limitation gets in the way quickly. Rather than allowing you to sync all your calendars from a single account, you have to either put all your events on one calendar within that account (a hassle if you like to organize by type of event) or pay for the even pricier Premium plan that costs $70 per year. It’s easy enough to adapt if you’d rather save the money, but I wish that the limitations were a bit less limiting.

That said, you can work around at least the digital upload restriction by using physical storage. In addition to having 64 GB of onboard storage, the VivKeep supports USB-C drives and microSD cards, so you can keep a copy of your photo library on a drive or card and update the frame’s photos that way. It takes a bit more work than just managing everything in the company’s app, but it’s a good way to ensure you can keep adding new photos even if your frame is low on storage. Note, though, that you can only use one physical storage method at a time, so you can’t have both an SD card and a USB drive active simultaneously.

Photo-sharing method: Unlimited Cloud storage | Storage: No onboard storage | Screen size and resolution: 15-inch LCD screen, 1600 x 1200 resolution | Photo orientation: Landscape or portrait | Video and sound: Yes | Subscription: No

Aura’s 15-inch frame, the Walden, is best for viewing photos from afar thanks to its large display. Images look vibrant and sharp, even when viewed from across the room.

On the software side, it works just like every other Aura frame: you and your family members can upload photos to it via the company’s app, sending over email, or syncing with your phone’s photo albums automatically. Setup only takes a few minutes, and you can prop it on a tabletop in landscape or portrait, or mount it directly to a wall with the included kit.

While testing the Walden, my neighborhood experienced several power outages, after each of which the Aura was able to quickly reconnect to my network and start displaying photos again. Since it relies on cloud syncing to display your photos, it won’t show pictures when your network’s down, but don’t worry about that too much unless you’re trying to stay off the grid or live in a particularly chaotic climate.

Photo-sharing method: Cloud storage | Storage: 16 GB onboard storage | Screen size and resolution: 10-inch LCD screen, 1920 x 1200 resolution | Photo orientation: Landscape or portrait | Video and sound: Yes | Subscription: No

While Aura has a variety of frames with different aesthetics, you can’t swap the frames out later. Skylight’s Frame 2, on the other hand, has four swappable face plates to change the look of the frame. It comes with a faux-wood frame as well as slimmer black, aluminum, and blue frames. To swap them out, all you have to do is pull the frame away from the magnets on the display and snap a new one in place. If you want a more bare-bones look, the Frame 2 looks good without any border at all.

Setup is fairly straightforward: You can email photos to your frame or upload them directly from the company’s app. Once you’ve already set up one frame, you can also port all the photos from that frame to your next one. Aura’s system, on the other hand, doesn’t allow you to transfer photos across frames without contacting support.

The Frame 2 has the same screen resolution as Aura’s Aspen, with a screen that’s two inches smaller, so its picture quality is a bit crisper. Images are clear and vibrant, and when a picture doesn’t fill the frame, the Frame 2 will add a nice bokeh effect on both sides. Skylight’s frames use touch screens for on-device interactions, which I prefer to Aura’s touch-friendly borders around the screen. It feels more natural, and it allows you to do more things, such as rotating an image or pausing on a picture you like. Unlike the first Frame, this model has a light sensor, so it will automatically adjust the screen’s brightness to match the room. Aura’s frames have had this feature for quite some time, but it’s nice to see Skylight add it as well.

Photo-sharing method: Unlimited Cloud storage | Storage: No onboard storage | Screen size and resolution: 13-inch e-ink screen, 1600 x 1200 resolution | Photo orientation: Landscape or portrait | Video and sound: No | Subscription: No

Because they’re designed to blend into a room regardless of decorating style, and they nearly all use LCD displays, digital picture frames can look pretty same-y. Aura’s newest frame, the Ink, stands out thanks to its unique e-ink display that gives photos more texture, sort of like a matte photo print.

Its 13-inch display isn’t quite as detailed as the screens on Aura’s other frames, but its newspaperlike look has a certain charm that feels more natural on a wall than a bunch of backlit pixels. Images of my niece and nephew showed enough detail for me to see their rosy cheeks and small details on their faces, but pictures with poor lighting suffer from things like dark hair blending into backgrounds.

That said, the e-ink display does more than just make photos look more analog. The Ink is the first Aura frame to operate off a rechargeable battery, rather than a constant A/C connection, so you can hang it on a wall without risking its cable being visible. According to Aura, the frame should last about three months per charge.

E-ink isn’t without its drawbacks, though. Unlike the LCD displays of the other frames we recommend, this one can’t refresh pictures immediately. Instead, it has to repeatedly flash aspects of the image on the screen, which isn’t fun to look at. You can only set it to change images once every 12 hours maximum. I appreciate the slower pace of the Ink, but if you want to see as many photos as possible each day, get the Aspen.

Photo-sharing method: Cloud storage | Storage: 8 GB onboard storage | Screen size and resolution: 15-LCD screen, 1920 x 1080 resolution | Photo orientation: Landscape or portrait | Video and sound: Yes | Subscription: Yes (for photo capabilities)

If you need to look at your family’s calendar as often as you like to revisit memories, get Skylight’s Calendar 2. In addition to being able to display photos in a slideshow, it serves as a household-management hub by showing all of your family’s appointments, events, and tasks on a central screen even kids without phones can check.

When you set up the Calendar 2 — it comes in 10-, 15-, and 27-inch versions — you can connect your Google, Outlook, iCloud, or Yahoo accounts. They’ll all show up on the Calendar tab. From there, you can toggle between day, week, and month views, as well as color-code every calendar so it’s easy to see who each event is for (you can make a profile for each member of your household). It works both ways, too, so you can create events from the Calendar and they’ll show up in your calendar app of choice. There’s also an option to set countdowns for things like vacations and birthdays.

To keep your family on top of everything, there’s a tab dedicated to managing tasks. While not quite as thorough as a dedicated to-do list app, it’s quite powerful. You can make single-instance or recurring tasks, or even set them as chores and routines. If one kid is on dish duty and another has to take out the trash, that’ll all be clear thanks to the Calendar’s color-coding system. Additionally, you can add rewards to certain tasks, and kids can eventually turn those points in for rewards once they hit a set threshold. And caregivers will appreciate the ability to set recurring tasks for things like giving a loved one their medications.

That’s all powerful on its own, but if you pay for the Plus plan ($79 per year), you unlock some more useful features. If your kids get a lot of physical invitations to birthday parties and events, you can scan them into Skylight’s app and they’ll automatically be converted into events on your calendar.

That also works with recipes. You can scan photos of handwritten recipes or those from a cookbook, and Skylight will automatically turn it all into a step-by-step recipe on the screen. I tried this with a soup recipe my grandmother wrote down for me before she passed. Her writing was quite atrocious, so I’ve had a hard time deciphering it. Skylight’s software had no such struggle. Within less than a minute, I could access the recipe right from my Calendar.

One issue: The ability to use the Calendar as a picture frame is locked behind that Plus subscription. It’s not too costly compared to a Spotify or Netflix subscription, and the added functionality that comes with the subscription is genuinely useful. But it does add to the cost of the Calendar, and other frames like the Aura (or even Skylight’s own Frame) don’t require a subscription at all.

Photo-sharing method: Cloud storage | Storage: No onboard storage for photos | Screen size and resolution: 7-inch LCD screen, 1024 x 600 resolution | Photo orientation: Landscape | Video and sound: Yes | Subscription: No

The ultracompact, freestanding Google Nest Hub is the digital frame I’ve kept in my kitchen for a few years. It’s marketed as a smart display, but that just means it can easily go from a slideshow of my family photo album to playing a YouTube video while I cook or showing me what’s playing on Spotify. It’s especially useful if you have limited space in your home for an extra gadget.

Even without all that functionality, the Hub’s crisp, vibrant display just makes photos look great. My kitchen gets a lot of natural light, but even on a bright, sunny day, the Hub’s display (which automatically adjusts brightness and color temperature) never gets too washed out.

Predictably, it’s easiest to link the Hub to a Google Photos account, though you may need to pay for additional storage in Google Drive to make room for all your pictures. And because it’s a smart hub, you can use it to check the weather, set timers, and control lights or other connected devices in your home. Like the Skylight Calendar, you can access your calendar from the Nest Hub, but unlike the Skylight, it doesn’t actually show your events on screen. Instead, it’ll ask you to confirm your identity via voice to avoid any privacy issues, then read out your calendar events. It’s not as convenient, especially for managing a family’s worth of calendars, but it’s a nice added bit of functionality to an already feature-packed device.

In addition to its impressive capabilities as a picture frame, its speaker sounds great for jamming to a playlist while you cook dinner or kick back and relax. It won’t compete with a more audio-focused smart device like Apple’s HomePod or Amazon’s Echo Studio, but if you want a speaker that can show all your best photos while you listen to your favorite playlist, the Nest Hub can’t be beat.

Do note, though, that since it doubles as a smart display/speaker, it’s always listening for its “wake word.” If you’re particular about your home’s privacy, it’s probably best to stick with a dedicated frame.

• Jen Trolio, Strategist senior editor

entry.title: Hot Wheels, American Girl, LEGO: The Best Advent Calendars for Kids (So Far)
entry.summary: Filled with building toys, science experiments, collectibles, and everything in between.
entry.content:
Even in this economy, the Advent calendar industrial complex is thriving. Sure, it’s still pretty early, but some of this year’s most popular Advent calendars for kids — particularly from NeeDoh and various other squishy brands, LEGO, Clickeez, Wigglitz, Pokémon, Fuggler, and Crazy Aaron’s Thinking Putty — have either started to sell out or are going fast. So it’s definitely worth planning ahead.

If you know a child with their heart set on a NeeDoh Advent calendar this year, your best bet is to stop in at your local independent toy store to inquire about availability and restocks. You can also keep an eye on the NeeDoh calendar at Amazon, just don’t get your hopes up too high, as restocks are haphazard and available to purchase by lottery only — if you get lucky and happen to refresh the product page at the right moment, you may be able to “request an invite” for a chance to buy the calendar at an unspecified future date.

Otherwise, to help you choose from all the other amazing Advent calendars available for kids this year, I’ve pulled together a list of favorites for all ages, filled with building toys, stuffed animals, crafts, collectibles, and everything in between.

Updated on October 29, 2026
I added several new Advent calendars and confirmed the pricing and availabity of all the ones we recommend.

Designed for toddlers, Haba’s Advent calendar is filled with 24 wooden animal figures and comes with a book that tells a daily story about each day’s animal. The box folds out to reveal an illustrated play area for the menagerie.

Strategist senior editor Winnie Yang and her number-obsessed 3.5-year-old son have been making their way through the Numberblocks Advent calendar early, to help with preschool motivation and good behavior.

Fresh pots of Play-Doh are always useful, and this calendar has 24 of them, plus a new tool every day to go with each new color.

My car-fiend preschool kid would love this holiday-themed Hot Wheels Advent calendar. Each compartment is filled with either a 1:64-scale vehicle or a festive accessory for a vehicle, like reindeer antlers or a Santa hat.

My son and I are obsessed with Monster Jam’s blind-bag mini monster trucks because they are cute and surprisingly satisfying to push down a ramp or flexible race track — the wheels spin very fast! This Advent calendar variation will net you 16 mini monster trucks plus nine figures and accessories. Plus the packaging turns into a mud- and snow-filled arena with a 3-D cardboard jump so kids can re-create the fun of a real Monster Jam show.

If you’d rather add your own gifts and treats to an Advent calendar, this capacious Step2 gingerbread house is a great option for little kids. Each drawer is big enough for a small stuffy, an action figure, or a toy car.

Kids who love exploring Busytown will enjoy popping out a new scene each day to create Christmas ornaments for a tree, wreath, or garland. The calendar comes with gold thread for stringing each ornament.

Rather than having them open a new toy or treat each day, Melissa & Doug’s countdown calendar lets children add a new wooden ornament to their tree. Each one has a poem on the back that parents can read aloud.

Nostalgic parents like me who read the Little Miss and Mr. Men books as kids will love watching their kids open a wacky figurine or accessory each day.

Here’s one that’s perfect for Disney Princess–obsessed kids. The box transforms into a wintery castle with a cozy fireplace and foldout furniture, and you get three princesses, Tiana, Belle, and Rapunzel, plus accessories and animal friends for each.

You don’t actually have to be a fan of Jurassic Park to enjoy this Advent calendar. Any dinosaur-loving kid will appreciate the chance to open 19 miniature dinosaurs, one keeper, and four set pieces that together create the stage for tons of imaginative play.

The Wigglitz Advent calendar is mostly sold out online, but you can still find it at a couple of independent toy stores (just don’t dillydally). It comes with 24 holiday-themed creatures, one of which is extra special and shiny.

If you’ve got a kid who loves board games, especially Monopoly, this Advent calendar is full of holiday-themed Monopoly tokens to liven up the basic set — from a pink penguin to a gingerbread Monopoly Man — plus a bright red display to house them all.

Here’s an Advent calendar for your kid’s American Girl doll to open each day. It comes with 24 doll-size surprises, including sunglasses, hair accessories, a toy cell phone, snacks, and a purple beanie.

I like the idea of activity-based Advent calendars that won’t add toy clutter to a kid’s room. This one comes with 24 mini kawaii coloring books.

This Where’s Waldo calendar is also filled with mini-books, but instead of coloring, each one provides a different search-and-find challenge.

Each year, LEGO releases a handful of highly anticipated Advent calendars. My favorites of this year’s cohort are the LEGO Friends calendar set in a snowy ski chalet and the LEGO City calendar depicting Santa’s workshop.

While it’s not explicitly billed as an Advent calendar, this elaborate LEGO Christmas tree set comes with 24 bags of bricks inside the box, so families can chip away at the build as they count down to Christmas Day. Strategist senior editor Jen Trolio and her family will be doing just that this year. Just be aware this set will likely sell out fast, so if you want to buy one, don’t wait.

Each section of this 25-day countdown to Christmas includes a holiday-themed mini-build with illustrated instructions.

This Magna-Tiles calendar has everything you need to build a Christmas train out of microMags. And the box folds out into a play set with train tracks.

Similarly, the PicassoTiles Advent calendar lets you build a festive gingerbread house.

Bluey fans will delight in opening a new figurine or accessory each day, including Bluey, Bingo, and Bartlebee as well as a buildable Christmas tree. Or if you’re looking for a little more razzle dazzle, there’s also a special Fuzzies edition that features flocked figurines.

Or you could get this Bluey jewelry Advent calendar with charms to build a bracelet and a necklace.

This New York City Ballet–themed keepsake box is my favorite of all the kids’ Advent calendars so far. Inside, you’ll find five paper characters from The Nutcracker to pose as you like. On top of that, the 24 compartments hold a gold-tone charm bracelet and an assortment of Nutcracker charms to go on it.

I also like this DIY-beaded-bracelet Advent calendar that’s much more affordable.

Here’s a putty-filled Advent calendar for anyone who can’t get their hands on the one from Aaron’s Crazy Thinking Putty.

Magic is a hobby that lends itself well to the Advent-calendar format. This National Geographic calendar comes with 24 magic tricks for kids to learn and the tools they need to pull them off.

Trolio’s two daughters have enjoyed this Thames & Kosmos calendar in past years. It contains all the materials kids need to do a new mini science experiment each day.

KiwiCo has multiple project-based Advent calendars, but this battery-powered winter wonderland for older kids is by far my favorite. It has a conveyor belt that helps sledders climb up a snowy hill, real working string lights, and an ice rink that shows skaters’ tracks.

Crafty kids get to make a dozen different cross-stitch ornaments with this Advent calendar.

For the many squishy hunters out there, this Squishmallows Advent calendar comes with 24 holiday Squish-a-longs that can each be worn as a ring.

Or here’s one for the Squishmallow traditionalists, with 24 mini winter- and holiday-themed Squishmallows, including a hilarious holiday ham.

You’ll get several “full-size” Fugglers, a few minis, and an assortment of stickers and other accessories in this 24-day Advent calendar devoted to the creepy yet kind of irrisistable creatures.

Inside this calendar, you’ll find ten Star Wars Bitty Pop vinyl figures, plus stackable cases and accessories to build your own Christmas-tree-shaped display.

This Pokémon Advent Calendar looks kind of like a coffee table book and opens to reveal a scene where kids can set up the pop-up tree, 24 days’ worth of ornaments featuring different Pokémon, and tree topper.

You’ll have to temper your expectations with this one: NeeDohs are still in great demand, and it’s extremely difficult to buy authentic ones online. If you are hoping to get a NeeDoh Advent calendar this year, your main strategy should be to haunt your local independent toy store and inquire often about availability and restocks. However, you can also keep an eye on the calendar at Amazon. Just don’t get your hopes up too high, as restocks are haphazard and available to to purchase by lottery only — if you get lucky and just so happen to refresh the product page at the right moment, you may be able to “request an invite” for a chance to buy the calendar at an unspecified future date.

Not technically an Advent calendar, but Taba Squishy is another popular squishy brand, and this case contains all 12 of this year’s holiday blind boxes, so you could start in mid-December and open one each day until Christmas.

Strategist writer Bella Druckman included this beauty-focused Advent calendar in her guide to the best Advent calendars for Gen Z because it feels curated by an actual teen. It’s got Starface pimple patches, a travel-size bodywash from Sol de Janeiro, and a mini version of the Billie Eilish perfume that topped wish lists last year.

Though it’s just ten days long, the Tonymoly x Squishmallows Advent calendar contains a nice mix of adorable and actually good bath and body products.

﻿Anthropologie’s embroidery Advent calendar also made Druckman’s list of good Advent calendars for Gen Z. Each day you embroider a new picture onto the calendar to fill out a holiday sampler over the course of a whole month.

Artsy tweens will appreciate the paint markers, mini-watercolors, travel paintbrush, and other arts and crafts in this city-shaped 24-day Advent calendar.

Another one for the crafty set, with materials to make a tiny roast turkey, gingerbread house, and more.

This slim Advent calendar comes with 12 days of darling Miffy sticker sheets.

Transport your kid to Tokyo with this extra-large 30-day Japan-themed Advent calendar featuring snacks, accessories, toys, stationery, and home goods.

Except for the first one, the doors on this Advent calendar aren’t numbered. Instead, each day, you must solve a new riddle, the solution to which will tell you which door to open next in an intergalactic race to celebrate Christmas.

Similar to the Exit calendar above, to solve the mystery at the end of this Clue-themed Advent calendar — and move on to the following day — you must solve riddles and crack codes behind each door. This is an excellent collaborative Advent calendar for families who love murder mysteries.

But if Dungeons & Dragons and other role-playing games are more your kid’s speed, this polar-bear-themed Advent calendar is full of festive dice that’ll make any gamer smile.

A Strategist favorite, the Bonne Maman Advent calendar contains 24 limited-edition spreads and jams to share and discuss each morning with family.

The Haribo Advent calendar is a real crowd-pleaser with a new pack of delicious gummies to open each day. You’ll just need to make a plan to deal with any sibling fights that erupt over the best ones.

In this ugly-sweater-themed Advent calendar, you get 25 different kinds of gourmet marshmallows. Each day is a surprise, with a clue to help you guess the flavor before opening.

For tween and teen baking enthusiasts, this calendar is full of cookie cutters, spatulas, piping bags, and more tools to make professional-grade holiday cookies.

This six-day calendar is a great intro to makeup for tweens and teens who love Snoopy. It comes with a freckle pen, highlighter stick, scented lip mask, scrunchie, compact mirror, and Snoopy plush keychain.

entry.title: What Trichologist and AWARE Hair Founder Tina Mui Buys at the Drugstore
entry.summary: “I call it a tiny little tube of miracle.”
entry.content:
Here at the Strategist, we love hearing about everyday stuff that actually works. That line of thinking extends to the drugstore beauty products in our medicine cabinets, shower caddies, and makeup bags. In our series “Beauty Aisle,” we talk to folks in the beauty industry — aestheticians, hairstylists, makeup artists, dermatologists, and the like — about the go-to affordable products they keep stocked. For this installment, Strategist beauty writer Kitty Guo chatted with Tina Mui, trichologist and founder of the hair-care brand AWARE Hair, about the drugstore products she loves.

I’ve been using this forever. It’s super-nice because it’s an oil-free makeup remover but it can remove all traces of eye makeup, including kohl liners that you put in your waterline and waterproof mascaras. I love how it doesn’t irritate sensitive eyes because mine are supersensitive. I’ve used it for maybe 20 years, so it’s tried and true. It’s on subscription.

Even if you take off your makeup with the remover, it still leaves remnants sometimes. And if you leave those in your eyes overnight, they actually may cause damage. So it’s really important for me to end the day with some eye drops that remove the residue. I do think it’s a step that people miss, and later on they have eye infections. I actually had an infection one time that burned my cornea, so now I’m supersensitive about making sure I keep my eyeballs clean.

I really like this Visine one because it doesn’t burn. It’s very soothing at the end of the day. I really recommend people use an eye drop, especially women because we put on makeup, to get it fully off your eyes.

I’ve tried all kinds of moisturizers and body creams, and usually they’re too greasy or heavy. This one’s just right. I use it after a shower, and it absorbs easily and feels very light on the skin. You feel hydrated but not greasy. It’s blended with some great ingredients: rich botanical oils, shea butter, squalane, plant-based peptides. It has a firming effect, so it makes the skin feel tighter but not uncomfortable; it just makes your skin feel more youthful. And it has a natural fragrance, not synthetic — a very light vanilla-coconut scent. I think most people would like it if they tried it.

I’ve tried all kinds of expensive cleansers, but I come back to this one. I use it morning and night. It’s very gentle. I have normal to dry skin, so it makes my skin feel really clean and hydrated, and it gets the makeup and foundation off without making my skin feel tight and stripped afterward. It maintains your skin’s natural moisture barrier and pH level. And it’s fragrance free, sulfate free, and paraffin free, and that’s really important to me.

I’ve been looking for an SLS-free toothpaste, and this one is. It’s also fluoride free, but I haven’t gotten any cavities. It’s crafted from naturally derived and naturally sourced ingredients, which I love. It has a very pleasant peppermint taste that’s not overly strong. I’ve been using it for the past year or so, and now it’s my favorite.

I’ve tried all brands of liquid liners because I like to do a cat eye. This one has been a staple. Interestingly, it’s not a liquid liner; it’s a pencil, but it works really well. The cream formula glides on easily and creates a perfect line. You don’t even need a pencil sharpener because this sharpens like a mechanical pencil. And it doesn’t smudge — that’s most important to me. It’s very pigmented like a liquid liner, but it’s very easy to apply. It works fast and gets the job done.

I don’t actually use this on my face because I put on SPF before I put on my makeup. But it’s handy to travel with because sometimes you just need sunscreen. If you happen to be outside and your arms or legs are exposed, it’s important to put on sun protection and not get burned. I keep it in my purse in case I’m caught out in the sun. It’s in a little spray bottle, and it’s easy because you can spray it on and you don’t have to get your hands full of sunscreen. It has UVA and UVB protection, and it’s very light, not greasy.

After Bite to me is like a hack. Some people never get bitten, but for some reason, mosquitoes love me and I get welts. This little tube is a lifesaver. I call it a tiny tube of miracle because it stops the itching. It’s really important not to scratch because the more you scratch, the more irritated it gets. You put this on right away, and I don’t know if it’s healing the bite but it really stops you from making it more irritated.

I don’t know how diligent people are about cleaning their brushes, but I’m a cosmetologist and trichologist so those things really matter to me. I highly suggest people clean all their brushes at least every couple of days because brushes can develop mold. This particular cleaner is gentle, fragrance free, sulfate free, and doesn’t have any harsh chemicals. It cleans your brushes without leaving a residue. If you have it handy, you will tend to clean your brushes more often. It’s so easy to just pour it on your brush, rinse it out, let it dry overnight, and then it’s ready for you the next day.

The plastic Wet Brush is so popular, but this particular one has a synthetic boar bristle that emulates a natural boar bristle and helps remove impurities from your hair. Pollution, lint, whatever — it really removes everything. I have long hair, and this brush helps to reduce frizz and detangle without ripping the hair. Sometimes, those plastic or metal brushes can scratch or irritate your scalp, but these bristles are comfortable and feel gentle.

I’ve used this in the salon, but I also use it personally. I’ve had this brush for over a year. I think it works for all hair types. Even if you have really curly hair that gets tangled, you can just start at the ends and work your way up to the roots.

entry.title: What Eric Sze Can’t Cook Without
entry.summary: “It’s like the Heinz ketchup of Taiwan.”
entry.content:
If you’re like us, you’ve probably wondered what everyday stuff famous people add to their carts — like mascara or a sleep mask. In this iteration of our “Celebrity Shopping” column, we’re asking food-obsessed folks what they can’t cook without. Here, Eric Sze — chef and co-owner of New York City’s Wenwen and author of the just-released cookbook Taiwanese? — tells us about his favorite items.

Rice is a staple in Taiwan, as it is across so many different countries and cultures. The people there used to only eat long-grain rice. It was the only type available until the occupation, during which the Japanese dedicated a lot of resources to agriculture because they viewed Taiwan as sort of an agrarian state that could supply their never-ending war. In order to feed their soldiers, they developed a short-grain rice variety that could grow in the subtropical climate of Taiwan — the first of its kind. The Taiwanese population had the rice and was like, Oh my God, this is the best shit ever. And so they ditched all of the long-grain rice — well, most of it — and now the norm in Taiwan is short-grain rice. It’s bouncier. It’s got a higher starch content, so it sticks together more. Some would say that it’s fluffier, which it is. For me, it’s ingrained in my DNA: short-grain rice, short-grain rice, short-grain rice. Tamaki Gold is what I found to be at the crux of the intersection of availability, flavor, and consistency. It’s sweet, which is very important. And the aftertaste of sweetness really lingers. And it pairs well with food because you want the flavor of the rice to last as long as the aftertaste of whatever you’re eating. So let’s say I’m eating a stir-fry and something that is soy-sauce-heavy and maybe the flavors last in my mouth for about five minutes before it eventually subsides — the flavor of the rice also needs to last.

Yu Ding Xing is very accessible because, thanks to Yun Hai, it ships everywhere. Taiwan is a place where there’s so much abundance in fruit they can just add fruit to anything and it doesn’t really add to the cost. The pineapple here just adds a tiny bit of sweetness. It’s also a black-bean-based soy sauce. I want to stress that even when I was growing up in Taiwan, black-bean soy sauce wasn’t the norm. And it still really isn’t the norm in terms of household cooking. So to be in America and to have black-bean soy sauce so accessible is pretty wild. It’s so much earthier, light enough to use as a salad dressing. It’s still savory enough that you can use it in a stir-fry. You might want to supplement with a little bit of salt or regular soy sauce or a different black-bean soy sauce, but it’s so perfectly balanced. It can lend itself to any type of dish. Like, I’ve cooked boeuf bourguignonne with this soy sauce. I’ve cooked a nice ragù with this soy sauce. I’ve made a summer heirloom-tomato salad with this soy sauce with nice olive oil. It pairs well with olive oil, it pairs well with star anise and Sichuan pepper, it pairs well with cheese. It’s just crazy.

I grew up with this sauce. It’s like the Heinz ketchup of Taiwan. When you’re cooking, sometimes you’re just missing a little bit of something, you know? Maybe you’re too lazy or too hungover to really sit down and think about what is missing. As long as it’s in the savory field, almost 9.5 times out of 10, you can just dollop a scoop of this super-savory shallot sauce and it’ll make things a hundred times better. Imagine it’s a chili crisp without spicy chili. It’s all shallots. It’s lightly pasty, crunchy, crispy. Sometimes when I’m sautéing and sweating shallots and I don’t want to wait too long, I just add a dollop of this and save myself 15 minutes.

Because there are no eggs in these noodles, they’re not super stiff. They take, like, three minutes to cook instead of ten minutes like pasta and hold up very well to sauce. The wheat is a regular white flour instead of semolina, so it’s not as inherently flavorful, but it is a great way to add al dente texture into anything you want. In the summer, I make cold noodle salads with them. In the winter, I add them to soups. It’d be weird to add spaghetti into a Chinese soup, but it’s not weird to add this noodle into a Bolognese.

I can no longer cook without this. I recognize it’s pretty artificial, which I don’t typically like, but I make an exception for this. The flavor is very nostalgic to me. I didn’t realize how much Hondashi is used in Taiwanese street food until I really started studying Taiwanese food. Everything is Hondashi plus celery. I grew up with that note of almost smoky, fishy flavor that was really ingrained into my subconscious. Any time I’m making a stir-fry, as long as it makes sense that there’s fish in it, I add Hondashi. If I’m making a vongole, I will add Hondashi. I’ll use it to make a dashi broth. It’s like a seasoning salt.

Thanks to MáLà Project, everybody loves Sichuan peppercorns. I shamefully cannot eat that spicy, and every time I visit MáLà Project, which I do frequently, I have a terrible time sleeping, for obvious reasons. But I do love the má in the Sichuan peppercorn. The là — the spice — is no longer part of my life. But the má — the floral notes that don’t linger on the other end of your body — is what I really like. There are two types of Sichuan peppercorns: red and green. The red is a little bit more earthy and punchy. The green is very floral and arguably more má. It provides more of that tingling sensation but is also lighter in flavor. So this green Sichuan peppercorn oil I love adding to cold dishes. I use it sometimes as an olive-oil replacement because it has that same note of light fruitiness, but the middle palate becomes extremely floral and then it subsides into that light numbingness. I find that to pair super well with any type of vinegar. As long as your cold dish is a little acidic and a little sweet, it’s extraordinarily delicious. You can also drizzle it on pizza.

Fried shallots are a very easy way to add texture as a garnish. One of my favorite ways to use fried shallots is garnishing soups — they go crispy-soggy — because it actually seeps the flavor of the shallot oil into the broth. Just make sure the broth is a relatively clear one, like pho or Japanese chintan ramen. American chicken-noodle soup is very good with fried shallots. It pairs very well with celery, which is in chicken-noodle soup. You know what else pairs well with celery? Hondashi pairs very well with celery. So add that too.

During COVID, everybody was jarring their own sauce in restaurants with decent success. We sold at a lot of mom-and-pop shops, including the Meat Hook. Literally a week after we started selling there, they came to us and said, “The USDA looked at your product and said, ‘What the hell is this? It’s not in our database.’” Then they came to the restaurant and said, “This is not a production facility. If you keep selling this, we will shut both of your restaurants down.” We took that very seriously and stopped. But we took the recipe, went to Taiwan, had five batches made, and finally landed on a good recipe — because making one batch versus making 5,000 jars is very different. The difficult thing about manufacturing this sauce is that the chefs in the plant need to measure the water content every ten minutes because it’s not meant to be a super-crispy chili oil. It’s made with a base of alliums, heavy on garlic and scallions. We cook those gently for a long time until they’re starting to color but still have a lot of water, and then we add in our spices. Just when the scallions and garlic are beginning to dry out but aren’t fully, we pulverize the mixture so there’s a pastiness — like it’s almost spreadable. We put a lot of time and effort into that texture. It’s super versatile. It’s sweet, umami, savory, and has depth. It’s not too spicy because I can’t handle too much spice; it just adds a kick to your tongue. A little Kewpie Mayo, a little of our chili paste, some balsamic vinegar, rice vinegar, and a little bit of honey — mix that up and you have a perfect salad dressing. And for noodles: just soy sauce, vinegar, our chili sauce with plain old somen. Delicious.

entry.title: Matilda Goad’s Favorite Under-$100 Home Items
entry.summary: Rope doorstops, fly covers, and glass-polishing tea towels.
entry.content:
Design can be prohibitively expensive, but not far from, say, Julianne Moore’s George Nakashima table, there might just be a solid, economical Ikea shelf. In this series, we ask designers for their favorite useful, utilitarian home items under $100. This week, London-based designer and founder of MG & Co., Matilda Goad, who launched her holiday collection this week, shares her essential rope doorstop, fly cover, and glass-polishing tea towels. 

I’m obsessed with items in my home being really hardworking, so I’ve become quite ruthless at getting rid of pieces that aren’t serving a purpose and are purely decorative. I’m a bit of a magpie at heart, but also, I’ve got four other people sharing my home with me, and there’s only a certain amount of stuff. So the items have to work really hard but also be beautiful to some extent. And I think the pieces that fall through the net of not being really functional items have to spark so much joy.

I tend to veer back to these kinds of quite classic designs and materials. It’s a little bit of a nod to nautical, but they’re really classic, and this design has been around for years. It adds a punctuality of character without being overbearing.

I’m basically really obsessed with functionality. Increasingly so, as I now have three kids, I like things to just be efficient. So a bad knife is really bad. These Opinel knives are the everyday knives I use in my kitchen. They look cool when they’re in the drawer. I’ve got two different packs of them and they’re all different colors, and they’re just really good knives. You don’t want to compromise on a good blade. I’ve tried the Ikea knives and scissors in the past, and they’re not good. These are fun and they’re really good.

Cornishware — it’s a really classic design that I grew up with in England, and as children we always had the mugs and the jugs. I love this idea of decanting your milk on the table rather than a horrible, you know, plastic bottle on the dining table. And it’s in this classic, familiar print.

The washing-up brush from Salter House is just brilliant — you know, they’re aesthetic, but also there’s no plastic in them. It’s something I buy in stacks and keep the spare heads underneath my sink. I store it in a little brass caddy on the side of the sink, where I also keep my Fairy liquid dish soap. You don’t want them to sit in water. That’s when they go a bit icky.

I actually have never made it to their showroom in Brooklyn, but I’m obsessed with this brand. And I love the scissors. I love functionality in my desk drawer; I like to know where my scissors live. And it’s just a take on an everyday thing I really need.

A debobbler is essential in any laundry area; I’m obsessed with them. With a sweater, you sit and it makes it like new again. They’re amazing and really efficient. I find it relaxing. It’s a nice thing to do when you’re watching television or something.

Add a little to your floor cleaner; it’s very potent. I have wooden floors in my home, and it just has this really beautiful scent; it’s lavender but it almost seeps into the wood. It’s just a really nice way of adding a bit of fragrance to your cleaning. I try to stay away from scented chemicals, and this product is amazing.

I have toast every single morning with my family, and I like to have a little setup that makes a ritual of it. This bread board catches all the crumbs, but it’s really beautiful as well. I like to have a station with the knife just left there. The ease.

I actually have the full set: lime, lemon, and orange. It’s quite cool when you get them as a set, because they’re nested together. I use it every morning to make lemon tea — hot water with lemon. It’s a really great design.

Bread bins are really hard to find. I did a lot of sourcing because it’s very prominent in my kitchen, which is where my bread bin lives. But again, it’s a really classic design. I keep it where I have my chopping board for the bread. I like a bin over a box because you can cram quite a lot into it. And I love having accents of red or burgundy. It’s just this really nice pop of color in the kitchen.

I always have loads of fruit out, and I don’t like the fruit flies in the summer. It’s also brilliant when you are serving food. I keep it on an open shelf in my kitchen when I’m not using it; it’s genius.

I try not to buy stuff from Zara Home, since I have my own brand, but I have to put my hand up here and admit that they have done something very beautiful. I feel that there are quite a lot of designs imitated from other designers, and I think with the volume that they’re producing in, they’re able to really undercut pricing. But I’m a great believer in high and low, and in this case, I think it’s about bringing pieces into your home that you believe are going to be there for the long run. There are a lot of associations with Zara, that people buy in bulk and that the items have a very short life. Whereas I think if you’re buying a very conscious item, you know, that’s great.

The Niwaki clean mate is incredible at keeping your tools in shape, removing rust, and making them as good as new.

This is really, really sad, but I’m obsessed with these. I even bought them for my fridge in our studio. I’m quite obsessed with organization in my fridge, and I like to unpack any fruit or vegetables that come in plastic. I like to undo the wrappers and keep everything in these wire baskets. I do all my lemons and limes in one, all my apples in another. These plastic trays are really good because quite often the shelves in the fridge are funny heights and you can’t maximize the space. I seem to have to have so much food in my fridge with my family. I use one of these for cheese and sometimes herbs and smaller bits. When you’re trying to think of something to cook and you open the fridge and everything is organized, it’s really inspiring to be like, Oh, I’m going to cook with this and this and this. When everything is crammed in and you can’t see what’s in your fridge, it’s very uninspiring. These fridge trays are not chic, but they are life-changing.

I am obsessed with Josef Frank. I love to serve tea by the television or by the fire. I like to put everything on this tray and serve cocktails on it. It’s just this really fun print that I don’t think I could take in a bigger scale. I love that you can bring it out and it’s kind of a party on its own.

With my fridge obsession, you can wash all your fruit and then serve it straight to the table. It’s really purposeful, but I love that it can be out on show.

These are just, again, a really classic design. A bad tea towel is not great when you’re trying to polish your glasses and it’s all fluffy. These are the classic linen tea towels — you need to have a generous stack of them under your sink for polishing glasses and stuff.

It’s a really great scent. I keep it in the bathroom.

I like to have eggs out in the kitchen. I like to decant them from what they’ve come in. In my kitchen, I like that the food and the produce kind of punctuates the character and the colors within the space.

The large is really generous; it’s quite a big size. And there is one that is very skinny and very long and it fills a doorframe, which I think is really useful in an area where people are coming in and out and you wouldn’t necessarily have a doormat.
