entry.title: The Best Gifts for 3-Year-Olds
entry.summary: Toys to support language development, fine motor skills, and a lot of jumping.
entry.content:
As my son approaches age 4, the kind of play he’s enjoyed most as a 3-year-old falls into two camps: physical activities like riding a bike, climbing playground equipment, or jumping into a ball pit, and imaginative ones where he acts out (and narrates) different professions or scenarios like a barista making coffee, a train conductor announcing local stops, or a dinosaur teacher directing their students to line up.

According to Rebecca Parlakian, a child-development expert and senior program officer at Zero to Three, between the ages of 3 and 4 years old, children’s language and thinking skills are undergoing huge leaps forward. “They now are constructing whole narratives that they act out through pretend play,” she says. So toys and books that spark lively conversations are highly encouraged. Of course, not every 3-year-old wants to talk at length about the difference between bullet trains and steam engines; some are fascinated by mermaids, while others won’t shut up about race cars, buses, or garbage trucks. Meanwhile, almost all children this age love toys that encourage them to move their bodies, from a simple playground ball to a trampoline.

To help you find the best toys that will give the 3-year-old in your life a chance to jump, chat, and otherwise indulge their many evolving interests, I talked to professionals like Parlakian, preschool teachers, toy buyers, and cool parents about the toys they recommend. I also took stock of the toys my son and his friends and classmates got the biggest kick out of over the last year. The expert-approved gifts below are organized by price, if you already have a budget in mind. Otherwise, read all the way through to get the full picture of what makes an elder toddler tick.

Meanwhile, if you’re also shopping for children in other age groups, we have gift guides for 1-year-olds, 2-year-olds, 4-year-olds, 5-year-olds, 6-year-olds, 7-year-olds, 8-year-olds, 9-year-olds, 10-year-olds, 11-year-olds, and 12-year-olds — plus the Strategist Toy Hall of Fame, filled with all of our greatest hits.

Updated on October 28, 2026
﻿I added several new picks and confirmed the pricing and availabity of all the gifts we recommend.

Part dress-up accessory, part sensory toy, these glitter wands have become a daily obsession in my home. They can be used to make things magically
“disappear” just as easily as they can be waved around like a glow stick at a toddler rave. I have also found them useful as a calming toy that can help dissipate a meltdown.

Susie Allison, a mom, former teacher, and the creator of BusyToddler.com, loves gifting Kinetic Sand to 3-year-olds because it is so satisfying to play with. Kinetic Sand isn’t gritty like real sand — it has a velvety-smooth texture that’s easy to mold, and it’s way less likely to end up in someone’s eyes.

Strategist contributor and early-childhood literacy specialist Maggie Yolen recommends this set of alphabet lacing beads for children who are learning to recognize letters and how to spell their own names, two skills my son mastered this year. The set also helps kids practice using their fine motor skills, an important precursor to writing.

Read more: The Best Art Supplies, Sensory Toys, and More to Help Kids Learn to Write.

Stickers are equally great for fine motor development, and you can find themed books for every interest.

At 3 years old, Milk Teeth co-founder Rebecca Calavan’s son was so obsessed with Hot Wheels cars that he would even sleep with them sometimes. So she always kept a few on hand as cheap, small gifts, in case she needed to “negotiate a deal.” My son loves them so much we bought multipacks like this to use as potty-training rewards. They can also be used as stocking or Easter basket stuffers, party favors, or Hanukkah gifts.

Strategist senior editor Winnie Yang and I both bought Blu Track flexible race tracks for our 3-year-old sons this year. And both of our kids have spent hours launching their collections of toy cars down the two-sided tracks. I have seen them at multiple friends’ houses too and convinced one pair of fellow toddler parents to buy one for their kid after it occupied our children for an entire playdate this past winter. The track attaches to a window or tile wall via a suction cup and then can be draped over chairs and other objects to create more complex downhill fun.

Despite it being rated for younger toddlers (ages 12 months and up), this has been one of my son’s absolute favorite bath toys for months and months. It’s also my favorite bath toy because it holds his attention, doesn’t require me to do the voice of a toy car or truck, and gets him excited about “doing the laundry.”

Kwik Stix are a parent and preschool-kid favorite because they can be used on lots of different surfaces, from cardboard and paper to wood and plastic. Plus they go on smooth like paint with little effort and dry in 90 seconds.

Wikki Stix are kind of like pipe cleaners, except they’re made from string covered in colored wax instead of wire covered in soft fuzz. They are satisfying for this age, letting little hands create elaborate sculptures simply by sticking and twisting the sticks together. This tube of 24 makes a wonderful and mess-free on-the-go craft.

My elementary-school-teacher husband brought this 20-sided foam die home from work as a fun way to practice number recognition with our son, who quickly declared it his new favorite toy and insisted we bring it with us on a family trip. Then I mentioned it to Yang, who bought one for her own number-obsessed son. My family mostly uses it to play catch, all of us shouting out the number on top each time it comes our way. Little does our son know, it’s also encouraging early math skills.

Read more: Our 3-Year-Olds Are Obsessed With This Gigantic Dungeons & Dragons Die

At 3, children will often express a preference for — or maybe develop an intense obsession with — specific characters from books, shows, or movies. Whether they’re nuts about Bluey, Spidey, Elsa, or the gang from Toy Story, mini action figures let them create their own little fan fiction, screen-free, while keeping them entertained in restaurants, in traffic, and in doctor’s waiting rooms.

I have lots of tea parties with my son, who insists on actually drinking out of the cups. So around the time he turned 3, I went looking for a nonplastic set and settled on this stainless-steel one from Melissa & Doug. It comes with a teapot, sugar bowl, mini milk pitcher, tongs, and pairs of cups, plates, and spoons, plus a convenient storage rack to hold it all.

If you’re looking for a unique outdoor toy that’ll keep kids busy for long stretches, this one’s a classic. Kids jump or stomp down on the air-filled bladder to blast foam rockets into the air. Just be warned, it will draw crowds of other children desperate for a turn.

Mega Bloks are extra-chunky for toddlers with smaller hands and still-developing fine motor skills. This green energy-themed set comes with 92 pieces including four figures, two bicycles, an electric car, and wind turbines, all made of recycled plastic.

Strategist senior editor Jen Trolio told me about this monster-themed math scale that’s fun for multiple ages. “A friend of mine bought this for her twins when they turned 3 and says that her then-5- and -7-year-old kids were also into it because they were learning basic addition in school at the time,” she says. Whether they understand the equations or not, trying to get the two sides to balance out is a great introduction to early math concepts.

Read more: The Best Games, Puzzles, and More to Help Kids Learn Math

Dr. Roberta Golinkoff, a professor of child psychology at the University of Delaware and co-author of Becoming Brilliant: What Science Tells Us About Raising Successful Children says encouraging imaginative play and social interaction is a fabulous way to nurture any 3-year-old. We featured parent favorite Sarah’s Silks in our guide to the best expensive toys that are worth it because the high quality and open-ended nature mean they will last for years.

Super Smalls has been recommended to us many times; its realistic-looking play jewels and dress-up toys are a favorite of stylish parents and more than a few celebrities because they’re cute enough for adults to want to wear. These over-the-top toddler heels make getting into character easy and a lot of fun. Plus the clomping sound they make when a 3-year-old walks in them is hilariously cute.

You don’t need to shell out for a coding robot to gift a STEM toy. This simple wooden bug hotel, which is home to 13 realistically painted insects, teaches kids about science, math, and spelling. Kids can match the critters to their silhouettes on the shelf, learn where each one lives outdoors, and start to recognize their names written on the undersides. Plus each bug can be added to a tower of blocks or a bin of kinetic sand as toddlers imagine a day in the life of the snail, worm, or bee.

Though we also recommend them in our guide to the best gifts for 2-year-olds, DUPLOs are great for 3-year-olds as well — especially more advanced sets that give them lots of options to play pretend and licensed sets that feature their favorite characters.

I recently noticed this Buddha Board–esque magic canvas hanging on the wall at my son’s best friend’s apartment. I like that it’s easel-size and allows kids to make a “mess” while painting without truly making a mess because it’s just water.

A more colorful and portable version of the paint-with-water canvas above, Melissa & Doug’s Water Wow! reusable coloring books come with a paintbrush-like pen that you fill with water to magically “paint” colors onto each page; as pages dry, the colors disappear, so kids can paint them all over again. Sarah Gregory, a mom of twin boys and a girl, explains that as they play with the books, kids learn to feel a mastery over them, which 3-year-olds hardly ever feel with anything else in their life. Perhaps more importantly, she adds, there was “instant quiet in our house when they would get going on them.”

Last winter, my husband and I discovered the many wonderful (and chaotic) indoor play spaces that have popped up all over Brooklyn, which is how we also discovered these squishy stepping stones. My son was transfixed by the feeling of the liquid-filled discs under his feet and the way each step made the colors mix beneath him. The stones are also durable and long-lasting, as evidenced by the hordes of children I’ve seen stomping all over them.

When I told New York features editor Julia Edelstein that I was updating this guide, she recommended adding this Lakeshore Learning fire truck — “the epitome of a dream fire truck, with parts that move” — because it’s indestructible and lasted longer than most of her sons’ many vehicle toys. “Lakeshore Learning is an expert in classroom toys, so their stuff is truly well-made and easy to clean with no small parts,” she adds.

When toy historians look back at this moment in time, Magna-Tiles (and their many competitors) will surely rank among the 10 or 20 best toys of the era, and they’ll probably still be popular even in a hundred years. The magnetic shapes improve fine motor skills, spatial reasoning, planning, and, when a structure collapses, resilience. Once toddlers are hooked on Magna-Tiles, they can continue to add to their collection with a variety of expansion packs like this pastel castle, a construction site, a spaceship, and a set of racetracks — making the imaginative possibilities endless.

Parents and kids alike love the Toniebox, and now you can get the screen-free smart speaker for less money and in a smaller, more portable size. Like the original and the Toniebox 2, the Toniebox Lite plays stories and songs when you place a magnetized figurine, or Tonie, on top. And there are dozens of characters to choose from, including Elmo, Winnie the Pooh, Peppa Pig, Curious George, and more 3-year-old favorites. I have tested every iteration of the Toniebox to date, and my son still listens to his favorite Tonies on an almost daily basis. And I can’t imagine giving it up anytime soon, since the Tonies library now includes a wide range of chapter books from Captain Underpants and Ramona Quimby to Wings of Fire and even Goosebumps for older kids. The only drawback of the Toniebox Lite is that it’s not compatible with any of the brand’s interactive Tonieplay games like Guess Who? or Monopoly. But that is far from a deal-breaker in my opinion, since the audio offerings have always been more interesting.

Read more: The Toniebox Lite Is My New Favorite Toniebox

Nugget modular play couches come in lots of bright colors and provide ample cushion for active 3-year-olds, whether they’re jumping up and down, wrestling a sibling, or trying out gymnastics for the first time. Milk Teeth’s other co-founder Catherine Newell-Hanson says the Nugget helped her kids with spatial skills and imaginative play — lots of fort-building — while supporting their crash landings too.

But if you don’t want to devote quite as much space to a foam play palace, the brand’s Chunk play ottoman serves a lot of the same purpose as the original play couch but can also be used as a makeshift tunnel or a table and two seats for little kids. It also makes for a comfy bucket-shaped seat for adults. Or Nugget’s newest product, the Smore chair, adds unique shapes to the mix and can be embroidered with a name.

PlasmaCars promote plenty of outdoor fun, getting kids excited and keeping them moving — without any batteries or even pedals needed. They are great for exercise and help youngsters burn off energy for easier evenings and bedtimes. Former toy-store owner Holly Magelof says they always sold well and are durable enough to make great hand-me-downs.

The train sets in preschool classrooms and children’s libraries are often the most popular toys among 3-year-olds, and BRIO train sets are some of the best you can buy. This recently released outer-space train set combines two beloved preschool play themes, allowing children to build a space station and use freight trains to deliver supplies, then launch the large space shuttle with suited-up astronauts inside.

Kids go nuts for the Jungle Jumparoo and its detachable rope swing that can be used to zoom from one side to the other. My favorite thing about it, though, is the safety factor. Because it can’t create a double bounce like a traditional trampoline, you don’t have to worry about multiple kids jumping on it together.

You can certainly buy specific dress-up costumes to help your 3-year-old channel the characters from their favorite books and movies or reuse old clothing instead of throwing it away, says Golinkoff. But if you’re looking for a gift with more wow factor, this dress-up closet will delight them while also keeping everything organized. It has a garment rod, four shelf compartments, and a built-in shatterproof safety mirror so they can practice lasso tricks, spell casting, princess waving, or robot dance moves.

I recently added Early Rider’s Big Foot balance bike to the Strategist Toy Hall of Fame because of both its sturdiness and its ability to induce joy in toddlers and their grown-ups. It has hefty, knobby, air-filled tires and a shiny brushed aluminum frame that’s light enough for my son to drag up a few steps or walk up hills that are too steep for riding. We call it his off-road bike and like to take it on small grassy hills in Prospect Park, watching as he confidently races down them with his feet up. It also gets us tons of compliments, and because it looks like a mountain bike, I can tell it makes my son feel more like a big kid.

entry.summary: Plus Plasticana clogs now come in two more colorways.
entry.content:
For this week’s “Don’t Dillydally,” we’ve rounded up a range of newly released products we’re particularly excited about, including a Boy Smells and Madonna collaboration, kid-size Our Place pans, and Imogen + Willie and Wrangler’s second drop.

In case you missed the first drop in September, Imogene + Willie and Wrangler’s second release hit the shelves this weekend. The 19-piece collection includes cowboy-cut jeans, graphic tees, pearl-snap shirts, trucker hats, and more rodeo-inspired wares.

One of the quintessential Strategist clogs now comes in autumnal colorways. The French brand expanded its selection and now includes the Jam (which multiple staffers — myself included — are eyeing) and Relish.

Cool-girl athleisure label Relax Lacrosse (spotted around town by my colleague Kitty Guo earlier this year) teamed up with monogram brand Abbode. Personalize your own set of fun-colored shorts or track pants while they’re still in stock.

If you have a hard-to-shop-for host on your holiday shopping list, MG&Co. released its Gift List Collection this week. Both practical and whimsical, the roundup includes engraved matchbox sleeves, fruit-shaped bowls, ceramic clam catchalls, and more.

For the tween or teenage girl on your list, Kendra Scott and LoveShackFancy have come together in this 17-piece collection. There are bow-adorned versions of Scott’s classic necklaces and tennis bracelets, heart-shaped jewelry boxes, butterfly earrings, and more.

Ahead of the harsh winter weather, Canopy launched a new version of its portable humidifier. The device takes up three inches of counter space and is seven inches tall, making it ideal for sitting on a bedside table or packing into a carry-on.

A24 came out with a collection of goods to commemorate the tenth anniversary of Robert Eggers’s The Witch in time for spooky season. Unfortunately, the Black Phillip butter dish is already sold out, but you can still buy the felted wool Thomasin tree topper (for now).

The celebrities are cranking out the releases this week. To start, Boy Smells teamed up with Madonna on two limited-edition candles aptly named Confessions and Like a Prayer. The first leans floral with notes of raspberry, geranium, and rose and is rounded out with patchouli. The latter is slightly warmer with notes of velvet amber, oud resin, and cedar smoke.

And now the Gen-Z version: Singer Tate McRae’s fragrance line has expanded to a hair and body mist. The fresh woody scent blends bergamot, orange blossom, sandalwood, and creamy tonka.

I thought I had sworn off celebrity beauty brands, but something about Jennifer Lawrence’s hair-care line is appealing to me. So far, mes Beauty’s lineup includes a repairing mask, smoothing serum, and volumizing mist that doubles as an oil reducer.

Rumpl released new psychedelic designs for its original Puffy blanket and sleeping bag in an unexpected collaboration with Liquid Death. Both pack up neatly in a sack that’s made to look like a can of Liquid Death.

For parents who are fans of the Our Place pan, now you and your little one can match. The brand partnered with toy brand Lovevery on blue versions of its (adult-size) pots and pans and a miniature set complete with a silicone mat “burner” and tiny wooden spoon.

entry.title: The Best Artificial Christmas Trees, According to People Whose Taste We Trust
entry.summary: “It’s like a giant jewel in your living room.”
entry.content:
Let’s get the obvious out of the way: There’s probably no scent stick or can of room spray that will fully capture the spirit of a real Christmas tree. It’s a smell that immediately evokes images of gingerbread houses and peppermint candy canes. But that doesn’t mean having one is without its problems — from fallen needles and having to water it to figuring out the proper disposal procedures (or even dealing with allergies). That’s where the right artificial Christmas tree comes in.

With an artificial tree, you still get all the holly-jolly joyfulness of a real one without the needle-dropping expiration date. You might even save yourself some bucks for years to come (as long as you have somewhere to store it in the offseason). If it’s your first time going faux and you’re wondering where to start, you’ve come to the right place. I asked set decorators, professional organizers, interior designers, and all-around Christmas enthusiasts about theirs. You’ll find everything from a tree that starred in a Hallmark movie to another that’s a “profane pink number.” And if you’re looking for Christmas-tree decorations, we have guides to the best tree toppers and tree skirts, too.

Updated on October 28, 2026
﻿There are new recommendations in here, including the Balsam Hill Silverado Slim and Terrain Artificial Pre-Lit Alpine Fir. I added testing notes for the Balsam Hill Balsam Fir and updated prices and checked stock for all the other artificial trees on this list.

Available in 5.5-, 6.5-, 7.5-, 8-, 9-, 10-, and 12-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here): unlit, LED color + clear lights, clear incandescent lights, LED clear lights, twinkly light show, and LED clear fairy lights

In the artificial-tree world, Balsam Hill rules. Interior designers, set decorators, and Christmas enthusiasts all sing the brand’s praises, largely because Balsam Hill’s trees don’t look fake-fake. “Some trees just look like plastic,” says Erin Swift, founder of the holiday-decorating firm Holiday Workroom. If you want a hyperrealistic artificial tree, she says, “the answer is simple: Balsam Hill. Always Balsam Hill.”

Balsam Hill trees aren’t cheap: They start at $399 for a Norwegian Grand Fir and average between $549 to $599 for a Classic Evergreen or Vancouver Spruce. A Scotch Pine will cost you even more, at $1,199. “Buy on Black Friday” — when there’s a sitewide discount of up to 50 percent off — was an oft-repeated piece of advice I heard from my sources. The brand’s Amazon storefront often has markdowns, too. But the final price will depend on the tree’s height — many are available from 4.5 feet up to 12 feet — and the lights you pick (Balsam Hill’s bulb guide is helpful for this). Every Balsam Hill artificial tree comes with a storage bag — so you don’t have to shove your investment back into a cardboard box after Christmas — and protective gloves to wear while fluffing the branches. It’s also worth noting that Balsam Hill has branch samples to compare — buying the kit is credited toward your purchase of a full-size tree — and you’re getting a three-year warranty.

The Balsam Fir, which is inspired by balsam firs in Maine, is a best seller, and it’s the most-recommended artificial tree here. I understand why after trying it myself recently: Assembly requires a few minutes and the most work you’re doing is tweaking branches just where you need them to be. When I pressed down on the foot pedal that turns on the tree’s LED clear bulbs for the first time, I couldn’t help feeling merry and bright. Interior designer Betsy Burnham likes the ambience and decorates hers with ornaments including “the tin boats my son used to love as a little kid, the carved family of porcupines my daughter always hung together, and the mini Eiffel Tower that’s always too heavy to sit right, but we use it anyway.”

Available in 3-, 4-, 6.5, 7.5-, and 9-foot heights

Target’s in-house holiday line, Wondershop, is full of inexpensive trees. Because it’s a seasonal shop (like its Halloween Hyde & Eek), stock moves fast — and might not come back for the next holiday season. Thankfully, this Alberta Spruce has, and now comes in different heights: 3, 4, 6.5, 7, and 9 feet. In the old apartment of e-commerce consultant (and my former boss) Brittany Nims, this tree stood between her now-husband’s desk and the entertainment console in their living room, which was very small (even by Brooklyn standards). Nims packed on the sparkle while decorating it, adding mini disco balls, a glittery star topper, and sequined, faux-fur-trimmed skirt. “There’s something about a glowing Christmas tree that’s just so cheerful,” she says.

Available in 5-, 7- and 9-foot heights

“I used to be morally opposed to artificial trees, but my husband is allergic to pine, which left me no other choice when we moved in together,” says Carrie Wittmer, author of First Famous Christmas. Moving into a then-new apartment with high ceilings in 2023, Wittmer decided — after “several years of owning a pitiful but hardworking Target tree” — to get a nine-foot Terrain Alpine Fir (which comes in five- and seven-feet versions too). At Christmastime, it resides in a corner between her dining table and kitchen. “I think the best Christmas trees are ones that feel like they fit into the space naturally,” she says. “Once decorated, it feels quite full. Its slim silhouette makes my weird collection of ornaments stand out more than they would in a thicker, denser tree.” (Her holiday-scented candles “make up for the lack of Christmas tree smell.”)

Available in 4-, 6-, 7-, 8-, 10-, and 12-foot heights

Prop stylist Alexandra Massillon used National Tree Company’s Dunhill Fir for a food-service holiday campaign. It’s “reasonably priced and honestly looks really good,” she says. “I don’t want to say that next to Balsam Hill that it looks exactly the same, but if you have a gift for decorating a tree, no one will notice the difference.”

Stefania Orrù, director of production at Eater, used to own fakes that were best described as “Charlie Brown–y.” It was a YouTube video that persuaded her to get a Dunhill Fir. “It was a steal,” considering how costly an artificial tree can be, says Orrù. It arrives unlit, which means you can change out the lights as you wish. And the needles are “pretty pliable in terms of positioning,” according to Orrù.

Also available in 4-, 4.5-, 6-, 6.5-, 7-, 7.5-, 9-, 10-, 12-, and 14-foot heights with the following pre-lit options: unlit, clear, multicolor, and dual-color

As long as Carrie Courogen, author of Miss May Does Not Exist, has lived in New York, she’s “gone through all the pathetic-tree phases: no tree at all, lights on a random plant, tiny table-top fir.” When she started researching artificial trees, the Kingswood Fir came up on this very site (our writer Brenley Goertzen kept it between a couch and a fireplace in her old apartment). It’s ideal for Courogen’s studio apartment, where “I don’t have a ton of space for something big, both when it’s up and when it’s time to store it.” It has shed minimally between Christmases, but she’s “consistently surprised by how well it fluffs out in spite of its compact nature.” And it’s “comically easy” to set up, taking her no more than ten minutes of “maneuvering to get it looking in good shape.” For someone who grew up in a “very passionate real-Christmas-tree house,” it works. “It obviously gives fake tree during the day, but at night when the lights are low and it’s glowing in the corner, I’ll admit, it comes pretty close to the real thing,” she says. 

Available in 6.5-, 7-, 7.5-, 9-, and 12-foot heights and either clear or dual-color lights

Our writer Kitty Guo grew up with an artificial tree that her dad put up every year — and this year, she put up one of her own. Guo set up the Downswept Douglas Fir (sent to her by National Tree Company to test) a few weeks ago and says that it was “extremely easy” to assemble. The tree’s parts slot together in a puzzlelike way, and the branches fall into place naturally. “All you need to do is a bit of fluffing and you’re done,” she says.

The Downswept Douglas Fir comes in heights of 6.5, 7, 7.5, 9, and 12 feet. Guo keeps her 6.5-foot tree at the foot of a staircase and says that the “pencil slim” silhouette prevents it from feeling in the way, even with the tree’s tall height. You can choose between clear or multicolored LED bulbs for the tree’s lights. “There are ten different options that you can toggle between with the foot pedal, and the lights will change colors, twinkle gently, or flash quickly in a kaleidoscopic whirl,” Guo says. She’s been buying baubles to fill out the tree ever since it was delivered: “I can definitely see this tree being the centerpiece of my Christmas decorations for years to come.”

Available in 6.5-, 7.5-, and 9-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): unlit and LED clear lights

Massillon has rented Balsam Hill’s trees for shoots — and remembers the box for a Douglas Fir “was beat up because it has been used over and over for 15-plus years by me and every other prop stylist or set designer in NYC.” Maybe that’s because setting it up is easy, says Massillon: “I hate the other artificial trees because there can be so many branches that get bent and flat; it is a nightmare.” In comparison, when the parts of the Douglas Fir are stacked, “the leaves kind of fall into place … like an umbrella.”

Available in 4.5-, 5.5-, 6.5-, 7.5-, 8-, 9-, 10-, 11-, 12-, 15-, and 18-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): unlit, LED color and LED color + clear lights, and LED clear lights

The Vermont White Spruce is another Balsam Hill bestseller. It’s meant to resemble the true white spruces of New England. Strategist senior editor Jen Trolio, who was sent a sampler kit, says the branches on the Vermont White Spruce are ever-so-slightly darker with pointier needle tips than those on the Balsam Fir’s. Joanna Douglas, the former director of branded content at Vox Media, says guests always compliment hers for how real it looks. That was especially important to her, as someone who was formerly against going faux. Douglas praises the branches’ bendability, allowing her to arrange and rearrange them as needed. Hers is decorated with photos of her cats depicted as angels — they were once naughty, nibbling on the needles and sipping on trunk water of her real trees, but are now “completely disinterested” in messing with her fake.

Available in 4.5-, 5.5-, 6.5-, 7.5-, 8-, 9-, 10-, 12-, 15-, and 18-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): unlit, LED color + clear lights, clear incandescent lights, LED clear lights, twinkly light show, and C7 multicolor LED

Balsam Hill’s Classic Blue Spruce was featured on the set of Hallmark’s One Royal Holiday. Fittingly, the movie’s set decorator, Christi Whiteley, calls it “majestic.” Another fan is Lauren Ragan, director of ad operations at Vox Media. The real-looking needles on this tree take a while to arrange the first few times — each branch has needles arranged in a sort of fan shape, and they need to be pushed out and down — “but after some time, it gets easier and easier, my husband tells me,” Ragan says. After pulling the trigger on the “onetime investment” four Christmases ago, she hasn’t looked back. Ragan goes for a “nice dressing” of different-colored ornaments on the tree, a compromise with her husband. Her in-laws, who are big on Christmas, have theirs “doused in ornaments,” a tradition her husband embraced before.

Available in 6-, 7-, 8-, 9-, 10-, and 12-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): unlit, LED color + clear lights, twinkly light show, ultrabright clear LED, and starlight twinkle LED

This is the first artificial tree designer Jess Knauf has owned as an adult, and it’s a far cry from “the very plasticky one my parents had in the ’90s.” She says it’s a cinch to put together, and the branches have plenty of space for ornament hanging. “We will be on year six this year,” she says. During each of those years, she’s filled with her collection of “vintage, unfashionable but sentimental ornaments,” and that this year, her topper might be a new floppy bow.

Available in 5-, 6-, 7-, 8-, and 9-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): unlit and LED clear lights

If you want a realistic tree that nonetheless looks a bit frosty — and isn’t flocked — Trolio recommends Balsam Hill’s Sanibel Spruce. “It’s one of my absolute favorites of the handful of Balsam Hill trees I’ve acutally seen in person,” she says. Plus it “very much matches the product photo on the site,” which isn’t always the case when it comes to artificial trees. The tips of the needles on this tree are a bit lighter in color, and the branch tips are especially lifelike. “One of the more obvious giveaways that makes a tree look fake is how the needles look,” explains professional organizer Britnee Tanner. The Sanibel Spruce resembles the evergreen in her yard instead of the “loose, sparse, and floppy” look of other fakes. Trolio agrees: “There are a good number of tips per branch” with longer ends that allow for “excellent ornament distribution.” (An important note: It comes pre-fluffed with memory-wired arms that fan into place, according to the company, though Trolio notes that you should still plan to do a good bit of finishing on your own.) Even after a few Christmases, Tanner still considers it to be her best buy for the holidays.

Available in 6.5-, 7.5-, 9-, 10-, and 12-foot heights and with the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): LED color + clear lights, LED clear lights, and twinkly light show

This is the narrow version of Balsam Hill’s famed Fraser Fir (46 inches wide versus 60 inches wide for a 7.5-foot-tall tree). Selina van den Brink, a freelance set decorator, used this tree for the Oscar-winning film Green Book. She needed something that would last for the entire weekslong shoot and “wouldn’t drop needles while being decorated,” settling on Balsam Hill’s Fraser fir after doing a quick poll of fellow set decorators. “It just has all the characteristics of a real tree,” she says. “It’s not too perfect — with an organic quality to the manufactured branches.” It was featured in a traditional tree-decorating scene, with star Viggo Mortensen coming home for Christmas “just in time to celebrate with his family,” so “the tree was a very big deal,” van den Brink explains.

Available in 5.5-, 6.5-, 7.5-, 9-, 10-, and 12-foot heights; full , slim, or wide shapes, and the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): unlit, clear incandescent lights, LED clear lights, LED multi-lights, LED color + clear lights, and twinkly light show

Available in 7.5-, 9-, and 10-foot heights, and either of the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here): LED color + clear lights or LED clear lights

Most artificial trees break down so you can store them in a box. The Flip Trees from Balsam Hill are designed to “flip” open on a rolling stand for even easier assembly. (See a video of how it works here.) It’s a feature that prop stylist Andrea Greco considers a “game changer.” (It also helps her rationalize the trees’ price tags.) Greco has owned the Red Spruce for over a decade and also uses them on sets — for one photo op, she covered the tree in hundreds of handmade gardenias dusted with glitter and garlands of paper leaves. She likes the idea of decorating it with a New York City theme, complete with Chrysler Building and Statue of Liberty, vintage subway tokens, and a giant rat.

Available in 6.5- or 7.5-foot heights and a pink version

Another big name to know in faux is King of Christmas. Its traditional and nontraditional trees are similar to Balsam Hill’s (with cheaper starting prices). Trolio had the chance to try out the King of Christmas’s Duchess (in a now sold-out flocked Barbie pink, but the blue version is still available). The color makes an obvious statement, and the settings on the dimmable light bulbs are another show in themselves — including one that Trolio describes as “very ‘dance party’ flashy.” Because of the flocking on the branches, the tree looks much fuller. “Think of thickening mascara on eyelashes,” Trolio says. Beware that upon opening, the tree has a slightly musty smell and sheds during assembly. “It wasn’t terrible, but there was a decent dusting,” she warns. Luckily, it was easy to clean up any fallen flocking with a vacuum. Like Balsam Hill, King of Christmas includes a storage bag and two-year warranty on every tree.

King of Christmas also makes a tabletop tree with lights that remind me of little stars (I kept one on my fireplace mantel all of last December). But inventory is low, so don’t dillydally.

Available in 4.5-, 6-, 7.5-, or 9-foot heights

Once a traditionalist, Strategist contributor Ivy Pochoda “left the fake spruce and tinsel trees behind” for what she describes as a “profane pink number” back in 2021. Even though the tree seemed frivolous at first, it’s well made — sturdy and plush and “filled the living room with shiny pink delight,” she says. Fluffed to its fullest, it “swallows lights and ornaments” — Pochoda decorates the tree with string lights, silver garland, and vintage ornaments from Christopher Radko and Kurt Adler alongside boxed wine and disco-mirror-ball ornaments. She’s since become known as the “person with the pink tree” in her neighborhood. “People paused as they passed my window. They went out of their way to take a look,” Pochoda says.

Available in 5- and 7-foot heights with the following colors and pre-lit options: silver with white lights, gold with white lights, and silver with color lights

“I know it’s fake, but it embraces the fakeness,” says Greco of this Martha Stewart tinsel tree. It reminds her of the retro ones from the ’50s and ’60s: “You know, silver could look tacky, but this does not.” She covered “the whole thing in disco balls” once and is thinking of adorning it with peacock and peach ornaments this year, but appreciates that it could go undecorated. “It’s like a giant jewel in your living room,” she says. “There are no sparse areas — you have to fluff it out, but it’s pure silver.”

If MacKinley Jade Lutes-Adlhoch, writer of the newsletter Yeehawt, could, she’d leave a Christmas tree up year-round: “There’s no way I’d sacrifice having one,” adds Lutes-Adlhoch. “But I have zero room for a wide base anywhere in my apartment.” Not that it’s a problem with this Homcom tree, which goes in a “corner around existing furniture without having to rearrange the whole living room.” You “can’t use a tree skirt because there’s no extra room at the base” (her tree is between an armchair and dresser too). But it’s a price she’s willing to pay for convenience’s sake — and she estimates it takes about 30 minutes to set up. Another bonus: Her cat Tofu, who’d “be thrilled to vomit up pine needles,” isn’t able to climb it. “While the most tenacious of cats could certainly still figure out a way to break every precious ornament, my own cat gave up pretty quickly with this tree,” she says. 

[Editor’s note: It’s sold out now, but you can sign up to receive an email when it’s back in stock.]

Available in 6- and 7-foot heights, and with either of the following pre-lit options (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference): LED clear lights or LED multi-lights

Balsam Hill’s Fifth Avenue Flatback was the tree I used last Christmas. It’s convincing enough that I didn’t even miss the fresh-pine smell of a real tree. But the biggest selling point of the Flatback is that, well, the back is flat. You’re still getting all of the fullness of a real tree in the front, but this tree can stand flush against a wall. It’s ideal for small spaces like mine, where I can only fit a tree between my staircase and the couch.

I also loved that the Flatback assembled (and disassembled) quickly. Because I didn’t have to think about a full 360-degree view, I could cut down on some decorating time, too. Just note: You’ll want to measure the bottom carefully for a tree skirt — I used a standard-size 48-inch one on mine, and had to tuck it around the trunk rather awkwardly. But I’m planning on getting something better-fitting this for coming Christmas.

Available in 4.5-, 6.5-, 7.5-, 9-, 10-, and 12-foot heights with LED clear fairy lights (see Balsam Hill’s guide here, for reference)

This was the the first Balsam Hill tree Trolio bought for herself (after previously inheriting a hand-me-down in a different style). Though in the end “a fake is still a fake,” Trolio says she chose the “sparse-on-purpose, pre-lit” design specifically for displaying certain ornaments. “I have become a way too over-the-top-Christmas-ornament person. I own hundreds and can’t stop buying them,” she admits.

This Alpine Balsam Fir has a place in the corner of her dining room as a “theme tree” holding her collections of pickle and pretzel ornaments. Since the branches aren’t especially full, the wires for the lights are a bit more visible, so Trolio advises that you be extra thoughtful about what kinds of ornaments you’re hanging — and mindful about getting the right “drop.” (On the same note, she recommends using a tree skirt instead of a tree collar, as the branches don’t go very low on the trunk and a skirt does a better job of hiding the flat metal base.) As for assembly, the tree “goes together super-easily, and the light connectors are built into the sections of the trunk so you don’t have to plug them together separately,” she explains.

This miniature tinseled tree isn’t intended to be a dupe of a real Christmas tree, which is exactly why Trolio likes it. “It’s a shiny purple tree, after all,” she says of the “pink” one she owns, advising that the shade is much darker and more magenta in person. The tree comes in a rainbow of other hues as well, including white and turquoise. Trolio usually displays her three-foot tinsel tree in her daughters’ room, but thinks the style would be ideal for anyone with “a more kitschy aesthetic.” You can also get it in pre-lit four-foot and seven-foot versions.

entry.title: My Son’s Favorite Screen-Free Activity Is a Cassette Tape
entry.summary: It’s cheaper than a Yoto.
entry.content:
Most afternoons around 4 o’clock, my 7-year old son disappears into his room and I hear a sound I haven’t heard in 30 years: the clink of a cassette door closing, the hiss of a tape rewinding, and then the crackly, fuzzy, warbly sound of a British man’s voice introducing the title of a story.

Yes, these are audio cassettes, and they have quietly changed what independent play looks like in our house. Like most millennials, I spent my early childhood in a time before Audible, before podcasts, even before MP3s. I had a vast library of children’s tapes, and some of my most comforting memories are of lying on my bed on 110th Street, nodding off to Richard Scarry’s Bedtime Stories.

My kids have full bookshelves and we read together every night before bed. But that is different from what I had with my tapes. Listening to them was something I did on my own without a grown-up in the room. It symbolized independence, privacy, and self-sufficiency, and I wanted him to have that too.

Friends suggested the Yoto, but something about it wasn’t for me. It’s expensive. A full-size player costs $150, and story cards have to be bought individually for around $13 each. And the Yoto is still another smart device, more like a terminal than a toy, and it comes along with (predictably) an optional subscription.

It occurred to me that what I wanted for him actually existed, it just had to be bought secondhand. So I set off on an eBay quest. I thought of all the books I’d loved as a kid and began filling a virtual cart with classics, from The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe to Harriet the Spy to Matilda. One by one they arrived in our mailbox, some in chunky plastic clamshells, others in flimsy cardboard sleeves, the rest in clear plastic cases with at least one broken hinge.

He was hooked. Like Max in Where the Wild Things Are whose bedroom sprouts up a forest, my son found his room turning into a wardrobe to Narnia, a boat ride on Willy Wonka’s chocolate river, a trip to Neverland. And like Max, when the adventure ended, it was time for dinner.

What surprised me was how obsessed he became with the mechanical aspects of the cassettes. It took him a minute to learn which button did what, but I could tell immediately that he loved the feeling of popping open the cassette player and flipping the tape over when one side ended. If a part was too scary, he fast-forwarded it. If he missed something, he would rewind and listen again. I watched as he developed greater fine motor control, patience with small mechanical tasks, and a sense of order, reading labels and counting to make sure the right tapes were in the right boxes in the right order.

It took us a few tries to find the right cassette player. Cheap portable models broke easily and chewed through batteries. A boom box I liked for its 1990s design arrived cute but nonfunctional. Then we found the QFX Retro-38BT, a solar-powered, rechargeable shoe-box tape recorder. It’s a tank and has survived being dropped, stepped on, and carried around the house by its handle. It’s a radio in case he ever wants to listen to a game on WFAN, and it also records, which means one day he can make mixtapes of his own.

There is some science behind why tapes might be good for kids. In a 1988 UCLA cognitive study, researchers found that children who heard a story on audiotape invented more original endings than kids who watched the same story as a cartoon, proving a theory that audio asks kids to put in more “high mental effort” imagining the story visually in their mind.

Like anything with kids, tapes can go from a habit to an obsession, so we try to keep it to an hour a day. After that hour, he comes out of his room, blinking, back from wherever he’s been, and asks what’s for dinner.

Pro tip: The narrators are just as important as the stories! For example, you can listen to Paul Newman, Sidney Poitier, Kathleen Turner, and Matthew Broderick read D’Aulaires’ Book of Greek Myths.

entry.title: This Rugged Screenless Camera Can Go Where Retro Cameras Can’t
entry.summary: I’ve never had more fun taking pictures — anywhere.
entry.content:
Screenless cameras have gotten me into the mindset that I don’t need to obsess over getting the perfect picture. I can simply hit the shutter button and move on. And I don’t risk getting distracted by a ping or a bummer-ridden news alert every time I go to take a picture of a pretty sunset or my niece making a silly face. So when I found out that Nocs — maker of eye-catching, rugged binoculars and monoculars — was coming out with a screen-free camera, I immediately wanted to try it out. Since I started testing it a couple of months ago, it has given me some of the most fun I’ve ever had taking pictures.

Rather than try to replicate the retro aesthetic of an old disposable film camera (as many screenless cameras do), the Nocs Portal looks like a mishmash of the company’s outdoorsy binoculars and a GoPro camera: A chunky square houses the lens and a digital viewfinder, while you aim and shoot with a colorful, textured grip that wouldn’t look out of place on a pair of ski poles. And it doesn’t just look like an adventure camera: The Portal is more ruggedly built that its competitors, with an IP56 dust- and water-resistance rating and an impact-absorbent housing, so you can take it anywhere without having to put it in a protective case.

More important, photos taken with the Portal’s 16-megapixel camera look so good I’ve hardly missed taking pictures on my iPhone. On a recent trip to Kauai, I snapped several photos on the shores of Poipu Beach, all of which came out sharp, vibrant, and even with a hint of nostalgia thanks to filters that can — despite the Portal’s distinctly modern look — give you the same nostalgic feel that more retro-styled competitors like the Camp Snap and Flashback aim for.

The back of the Portal doesn’t have any sort of display, so you can’t preview your images before connecting it to another device like your computer or tablet, but it does have a digital viewfinder. The screen inside the viewfinder is pretty low-resolution, which adds to the old-school charm. Since the viewfinder is electronic, you can preview the camera’s digital zoom (up to 8x) and the effects of your selected filter in real time. You still can’t view images after you’ve captured them, so you can’t hyperfixate on getting the perfect shot, maintaining the snap-and-move-on nature of screenless cameras that makes them so fun.

On its own, the Portal is an excellent digital camera with a charming design that’s as fun as it is functional. But its most exciting feature is its ability to use Nocs’ binoculars and monoculars as a sort of telephoto lens. Using a plastic ring that fits over the Portal’s lens, you can place a monocular (or one side of a pair of binoculars) over the camera to snap photos of things from afar. It takes some getting used to. While lounging on the beach, I managed to spot a sea turtle hanging out on a nearby island. I pulled out my monocular, adjusted the focus, and watched the turtle for a little while before turning on the Portal and taking a few pictures. I hadn’t gotten the focus just right, so the photos turned out a tad blurry, but I still enjoyed the meditative process of pulling out the monocular, observing the turtle for a while, and considering the framing of my shot before even turning on the camera.

At $180, the Portal is notably more expensive than either the Flashback or the Camp Snap, both of which offer a similar screen-free experience (as well as similar built-in retro filters). But for your money, you get a more weather-resistant design that stands out a bit more than those other cameras, the ability to shoot 4K video, and a real-time preview of your filters so you know you’re getting precisely the shot you want.

entry.title: The Best Items to Stock for Any Emergency, According to Survivalists
entry.summary: Whether you’re bugging out or bugging in, these are the things you may want to have on hand.
entry.content:
Compiling a stash of emergency-preparedness items used to be a task many of us kept on the back burner — something we knew was important and we’d get to eventually. But eventually, we now know, might be closer than anyone thought. And while we’re not suggesting you start digging out an underground bunker and filling it with instant noodles, in the past few years we’ve come to learn that having a few things on hand before you need them will only help you, even if it’s just mentally.

Most preppers, like Oregon’s Afrovivalist, Sharon Ross, equate preparation with peace of mind. “Once a person is prepared during a disaster,” she says, “they don’t feel the sense of urgency to go shopping for supplies.” So if visions of empty store shelves still haunt you, have a nice, calm look at our well-organized, detailed list of emergency supplies to keep on hand. To assemble it, we consulted recommendations from the CDC, Red Cross, the Department of Homeland Security, and the NYC Emergency Management Department. But those agencies give you only general categories, and we wanted specifics. So we interviewed 22 survivalists, preppers, bushcrafters, homesteaders, and emergency professionals about their favorite things to always have on-hand — and their advice to make your bugout (or bugin) the best it can possibly be.

Here are their suggestions, broken down into categories based on your level of survivalist instinct. There’s a lot to sift through here, but you can pick and mix products according to your needs. For many, a leaner survival kit makes more sense than a military-grade one. “Simplicity is key when prepping,” says Prepper Press founder Derrick James. Especially as, in a worst-case scenario, you might have to haul all of this gear a considerable distance. “It’s really important for people to know what their limitations are,” says emergency preparedness expert Aton Edwards, author of the book Preparedness Now! “Don’t prove how strong you are by dragging around a 40-pound bag. Rage lift in the gym, don’t rage lift your bag.” And in any potential urban or wilderness survival situation, advises Steve Lancia of North Camp Survival School in the Hudson Valley, there’s one piece of gear you should always keep around: “A cool head.”

Updated on October 28, 2026
We’ve updated this list to make sure our top emergency picks are still available and correctly priced.

If you’re not quite ready to build your own bunker, check out our first-timers’ guide to getting prepared:

Most preppers keep two bags: a three-day bag and a two-week bag. While you needn’t get too hung up on that, it’s not a terrible idea to have something that you can easily grab that has everything you need in it in case you have to leave quickly. Bushcrafter Mark Christensen recommends a “quality rucksack, or even a five-gallon bucket, which keeps your emergency gear together.” Survivalist E.J. “Skullcrusher” Snyder (whom you might know from his many appearances on Naked and Afraid) likes the “tough and roomy” bags by Gregory, but if you prefer something more tactical, he suggests something by Maxpedition. Jim Cobb, editor-in-chief of Prepper Survival Guide and Backwoods Survival Guide magazines, likes the RUSH24 bag from 5.11 Tactical, saying that it’s “robust without being ridiculously huge.” And Lisa Bedford, a.k.a. the Survival Mom, loves the Presidio Tactical Assault Backpack from Flying Circle, because it’s “a very good size for teens and most women.”

Edwards suggests an alternative to traditional rucksacks: the humble folding shopping cart. “If you aren’t physically fit, then lugging around a fully stocked go-bag can be difficult,” he explains. “So a folding cart will let you move around from one shelter to another shelter.”

Survivalist Travis McGill, along with Thomas Coyne, the owner and lead instructor at Thomas Coyne Survival Schools, and a survivalist who asked that we refer to him by the pseudonym “RC” like Surefire flashlights because they’re virtually indestructible. They’re so durable, in fact, that some are specially designed to be used as a self-defense weapon, Coyne says. McGill uses the Surefire D3ft but admits “it’s totally overkill” and says you could also “get something that takes AA or AAA batteries since they’re easy to find and replace.” Even a small one for your keychain will do, says Mykel Hawke, a former U.S. Army special forces captain and author of several survival books. “But make sure it has a turn on button, not just squeeze on, for when you need to have light to work and be hands free,” he says. Cobb, Edwards, Snyder and Morgan Rogue of the prepper site Rogue Preparedness, however, prefer headlamps to flashlights so you can be 100 percent hands-free and there’s less chance you’ll put your torch down and lose it. Rogue likes Foxelli or Petzl, while Snyder uses a Black Diamond Spot 325. Cobb also pointed us toward Streamlight’s products, which “work very well and will take a beating.”

There was plenty of consensus here, too. Unsurprisingly, everyone likes a Leatherman, a brand that also came out strong on our list of the best multi-tools. “I am a big fan,” Snyder says. “There are many types to choose from to meet your needs and budget.” Coyne likes the Supertool 300. And John Ramey of the prepper site theprepared.com likes the Leatherman Wave+ because it “doesn’t waste space and weight on tools that don’t matter much in an emergency, but it’s versatile and robust enough to be a core survival item.” The Signal, which McGill uses, also includes a fire starter and a whistle. If your survival budget doesn’t stretch to Leatherman, Lancia pointed us to the more affordable knife brand SOG, which designs similarly compact multi-tools for half the price.

For most preppers, recommending a first-aid kit off the shelf would be like Julia Child telling you her favorite flavor of Pop-Tart. They like to put them together themselves so they can pack them with, as Hawke puts it, “some dressings for real trauma,” including tourniquets, Israeli Bandages, and, in R.C.’s case, zip-tie restraints, though he wouldn’t really say what those were for. That said, Coyne calls Adventure Medical Kits “the best first-aid kits on the market [and] definitely the closest commercially available to what I would customize for myself.” Survival Mom has a different preference, saying, “it would be hard to find better medical kits than those sold by Dr. Joe and Amy Alton at Doom & Bloom.” Their company offers a variety of kits that cover everything from labor to gunshot wounds. Whatever first aid kid you decide on, Mike Glover, crisis management and response expert and host of the popular FieldCraft Survival podcast, recommends you always maintain a 30-day supply of over-the-counter medicine (like painkillers, cold, allergy, anti-diarrheal medications) as well as any prescription medications. And another consideration, via Edwards: “There should be stuff for dental emergencies as well. Any kind of emergency that forces you to evacuate, especially in the city, you’re not going to be able to find a dentist.”

Most of our experts recommended Kaito shortwave radios. Coyne’s favorite is the Kaito Voyager because it’s rugged and water-resistant, has plug-in and solar charging capabilities, and is shortwave, which means it picks up broadcasts from around the world. “In an extreme global situation, an entire country may be off-grid, but someone, somewhere, will be broadcasting,” Hawke says. Edwards agrees that a hand-crank radio is vital: “You don’t know if the internet and cellular networks are going to work.” Snyder likes the Kaito KA500 Emergency Radio. “It’s capable of being charged via hand crank, solar panel, micro USB, a standard wall outlet, or batteries,” he says. “And it has a five-LED reading lamp, an LED flashlight, and a red LED SOS beacon light.”

Waterproof matches are the best matches, though our experts say lighters are better than matches. Rogue recommends carrying both, in case either fails. Edwards, Cobb, and Hawke like Bic lighters, but Hawke stresses that “folks should review fire basics [because] it’s surprising how many people don’t know how to build a fire once they have a light.” Coyne uses only UCO Stormproof matches. “Once lit, they cannot be put out,” he says. “They even burn underwater.”

Hawke, Coyne, and R.C. all recommend power banks (which can be used to charge phones and other devices) that can be charged by multiple sources, including the sun. While Coyne personally uses a (now sold-out) Kodiak brand power bank because it’s rugged, water resistant, and has an emergency light, he recommends several reliable options that will also jump start your car, and are extremely small, such as the NOCO Boost. (Coyne also likes OtterBox’s charging cables because they’re “super strong” and “won’t rip or tear easily.”)

Ramey is the one naysayer when it comes to devices that use solar panels. He prefers to avoid them, because “you don’t want your battery baking in the sun,” he says. After “deep field testing,” he recommends the Anker PowerCore 10,000mAh. He calls it “the right mix of ruggedness, size and weight, capacity, and performance.” Rogue also likes “anything by Anker” to “charge your phone or other devices perfectly.”

Coyne uses only Energizer, and Ramey won’t budge from his Panasonic Eneloops “because they last a long time sitting on a shelf,” and Survival Mom loves the ones from Survival Frog (no relation). One thing all of our experts agree on is that whatever batteries you get, they should be rechargeable.

R.C. likes anything from The North Face. Coyne prefers the Montbell brand. Unlike mummy-style bags, which taper toward the bottom like mummy wrappings, Montbells stretch and are “next-level comfortable,” he says. Hawke recommends a slightly more austere (and multipurpose) solution: “a large trash bag, like 55-gallon type, can serve as great sleeping bag, shelter, rucksack, float, etc.”

No big surprise here: Everyone likes wool. Get “a good, old-fashioned wool blanket,” says Snyder, because it’s “tough, breathes well, and keeps you warm, even if it gets wet.” He suggests an Army–issued wool blanket from a military surplus store. RC loves Pendelton, and Coyne likes the Jungle Blanket by Snugpak. He calls it “a next-level woobie” (military slang for blanket) because it’s “warm, compressible, and water resistant.” If you have any extras around and are stuck at home without heat, Survival Mom also recommends covering the windows of your smallest room with blankets to stay warm.

Edwards says you shouldn’t underestimate the power of a good night’s sleep in a stressful situation. Alongside a good blanket, “what’s nice to have is an inflatable hiking pillow,” he explains. “One of the most important things you need to do in a crisis is get sleep, because your body gets worn down because of the stress it’s under.”

A surprising number of emergency checklists suggest bringing a puzzle to give yourself something fun to do. But “forget the puzzle,” Coyne says. “A deck of cards is best.” Hawke agrees, preferring cards for their small size, portability, and the numerous games that can be played with them. Also, as they both point out, you can get cards with survival info on the back, turning your diversion into a mini cheat sheet. And don’t forget to bring toys for your kids, Edwards says, “because they’re going to be frightened.” Cobb suggests a family-friendly board game that will keep everyone distracted and entertained during power outages: “Having a couple of fun board games or something similar will go a long way to keeping everyone busy and their minds off the crisis at hand for a bit.”

Bleach isn’t the only cleaner that will do the job. Snyder says cleaners like Lysol and Pine-Sol also work to keep things “germ free so that everyone stays healthy and doesn’t get sick.” But if you like bleach, any unscented, unadulterated bleach is fine. “Just get some bleach,” R.C. says.

Now hear us out: It might sound extreme, but at some point, you’ll probably wish you had some food. Our experts all approach the food question a little differently. Homesteader Lisa Sutton and the popular YouTuber, Prepper Potpourri (both Michiganers, both grandmothers), are big fans of canning and dehydrating. These processes take a little know-how, but are ultimately very practical and sustainable, especially if you grow your own food. They both like the All American Canner and the Excalibur Dehydrator. If you’re not ready to make your own food, our experts recommend stocking your pantry with, ideally, two-weeks’ worth of non-perishable foods like canned and dried goods, and peanut butter. “Think of very very simple meals, like oatmeal, [and] meals where you can open up a can of soup or chili and pour it over the rice and have more calories and more servings,” says Survival Mom, who goes into more detail about this in her book. And make sure you get stuff you actually like: “Don’t stock up on beans and rice if you don’t eat beans and rice,” Sutton says. Cobb’s in agreement: “Store what you eat and eat what you store. Don’t go out and buy cases of special ‘survival food’ if that’s not what you’re eating normally — a disaster or emergency is the last place you want to add stomach upset to the mix.” 

If you want more variety and are thinking of supplementing your stock with freeze-dried food, Survival Mom, Prepper Potpourri, and David at Preppers Survive like Mountainhouse. Sutton recommends products from Thrive Life, “because they are real food, not prepackaged, high carb, high sodium emergency foods” like typical emergency foods tend to be. Hawke likes MRE’s (which aren’t technically freeze dried and which civilians can now buy), beef jerky, and meals from a company called Wise Foods, whose empty containers, he suggests, can be used as toilets. And don’t forget condiments, he says. R.C. recommends any junk food since it’s “full of sugar and preservatives and is good for survival,” if nothing else. Rogue suggests “morale-boosting foods” like macaroni and cheese, packaged cookies, raisins, dehydrated fruits, popcorn, and chocolate. And Edwards points us toward “high-protein stuff that’s not very heavy” like energy bars and trail mix. “Because when you’re in a crisis situation, you are going to burn more energy than you normally expend.”

Jessica Kellog of the City of Los Angeles Emergency Management Department recommends having one gallon of water per person per day for seven days, but R.C. suggests getting even more: “You can’t have too much water,” he says. “If disaster strikes, the first thing I would do is fill the bathtub or the sink with water to keep it as a reserve.” As Edwards points out, “any kind of emergency where you have to evacuate your home, especially in a city, would probably classify as something that would disrupt water treatment.” If you’re sticking to bottled, any kind will do. But once that’s gone, you need to have a way to resupply, says Hawke. There are many ways to purify water. The easiest ways are by boiling (you’ll need something metal in which to do that), with water purification tablets (Coyne likes these), and through various filtration systems. Hawke likes the Life Straw and the O-Zone Pen for individual use, and Rogue, Prepper Potpourri, and Survival Mom like a Berkey for something bigger. David likes LifeStraw’s one-gallon gravity bag that removes lead, parasites, bacteria, and chemicals. It can also be used as a straw alone, with a plastic bottle, or with in-line hydration bladders. If you need a smaller option, Survival Mom uses and recommends the Sawyer Mini. Edwards agrees that the Sawyer is “a really good filter, that’s one of the easiest and smallest to use.” 

Even if you have the ability to filter water on the go, Edwards says that in an emergency, “you’ll want to be carrying as many containers as you can.” James says that these Aquabricks are “the best semi-portable water storage containers” he’s seen. “They’re strong, very stackable, and come with an optional water-filtration system.”

The consensus seems to be for Heatsheets, which our experts say are the strongest and lightest options available. “There are more lightweight ones, but they rip easily,” says Coyne. McGill suggests getting this option, which is sized for two, making it easier to stay covered.

“Just get the loudest,” says Coyne, who also recommends whistles “without moving parts,” like this one.

Rogue says that hand warmers like these are a godsend, and Survival Mom likes this rechargeable, handheld option from Frog & Co. Or, for a more long-term solution, James suggests simply investing in “a decent pair of warm gloves.”

“When thinking of an emergency that would force New Yorkers to evacuate — like an earthquake — masks are important because there would be an enormous amount of particulate in the air, infused with toxic materials,” says Edwards. He, Coyne and Rogue suggest N-95 masks, which paramedics use to protect themselves from pathogens. Ross, on the other hand, suggests you go for a reusable P-100 respirator, which offers the highest protection possible, blocking out 99.9 percent of contaminants, compared to an N-95, which filters out just 95 percent of particles and isn’t oil-resistant. Lancia says it isn’t so paranoid to buy a full-face mask (“The more I watch the news, the more I’m convinced that we all need a high-quality gas mask and CBRN filter to go with it. Mira Safety makes some of the best.”) But, as Christensen points out, “even a wet rag held over your mouth and nose helps a lot.” For extra preparedness points: “I would also have goggles to protect my eyes,” says Edwards. “And I’d have work gloves in there, because in the case of an earthquake, you’re moving debris.”

There are four different classes of fire extinguishers for four different kinds of fires — ordinary combustibles, grease, electrical, and metal — and our guess is you’d rather not get them all. (For example, R.C. likes a sleek Blaze Defense Fire Suppression Device, but it’s not for use on electrical fires.) Your best bet is a standard home model, which is versatile and inexpensive.

“Every household needs at least one alternative way to warm and cook food and heat water, and a solar cooker doesn’t require storing any type of fuel, which is a huge advantage,” says Survival Mom, who recommends a simple, box-style model. She also likes rocket stoves, “highly efficient stoves that require only tiny amounts of biofuel,” like the EcoZoom Dual Fuel model. David prefers Coughlin’s steel-coated canned-heat stove, which is sturdy enough for heavy pots and has covered sides that block wind. It’s compatible with any canned fuel and folds flat when not in use.

Should you find yourself at home without heat, “seal off one room that has the fewest number of windows or anything that’s gonna allow cold air to come in, and put up a tent in that room,” says Survival Mom. A cold-weather tent like this one is a good choice, she says, since it’s both warm and small enough to fit in a small room.

“Plastic sheeting, or even a nice tarp, can have many uses: from collecting rain water to drink, to [making] a traveling shelter if you don’t have a tent [and] sealing off areas to keep out germs or bad air from coming in,” Snyder says. Edwards also recommends tarps as a tent alternative: “A tarp can provide a barrier from the ground, or become a shelter — tents can be a little expensive, and tarps are tougher.”

Snyder calls duct tape “a survivalist’s best friend” that he’s seen used for “everything from making cups to helping stabilize a broken limb to patching leaks.” He and Coyne both like Gorilla tape. Alongside duct tape, Edwards says you can “never have too much line” for tying things down, and recommends carrying a fair few feet of versatile paracord. Cobb agrees, saying that paracord is “the traditional cordage for preppers.”

Everyone recommends you have a plan, preferably written out, and, if not rehearsed, at least talked about and memorized by everyone in your family. “Because in those moments when you’re frozen in indecision, and you panic, you’re starting to make really bad decisions,” says Survival Mom, who explains that “what you put into place beforehand is going to help you make the best decisions in those very intense moments.” “To implement the plan,” says Kellog, “survival supplies should be stored in accessible places that are known to members within the household,” And you should know how and when to use all the items you’ve gathered and test all your gear. And be sure to store important documents, photos and other items all in one place. Rogue suggests a fireproof and waterproof bag for this purpose. Edwards adds that when on the move, you’ll want to keep those passports and birth certificates close to your person, rather than in a separate bug-out bag.

Hawke loves these and has found over thirty uses for them, examples of which are here and here.

Glover recommends that “people carry a stockpile of personal hygiene items in the event infrastructure and supply chains are adversely affected.” Both Rogue and David like alcohol-free No-Rinse Body Wash. And rather than carrying a stockpile of toilet paper, Edwards suggests packing a travel bidet, which will take up less space and be “a lot more sanitary.” In general, he says, “don’t short yourself” on these kinds of comfort items. “Because you want to be able to maintain your sanity. These are the little things that keep you sane.”

Have a compass and a mirror (Coyne likes this one, below), and designate FEMA locations and evacuation routes on your map.

Ross recommends you educate yourself about what you can and can’t eat out in the wild and suggests you get a book on the subject.

“For waste disposal,” Kellog says.

McGill suggests getting a 2000W generator like this one to keep in the garage in suburban areas so you can keep your refrigerator on and charge your phones in case of power outages.

McGill also suggests keeping five gallons of gas in your garage. “To keep it from going bad, you can fill your car up with it once a month and take the tank to get refilled with fresh fuel at the gas station.”

Rogue swears by a folding portable solar panel “that you can open up and place within sunlight to charge your devices directly from the panel,” she says. “They come with USB plugs, so phones and other devices plug right in. You can do it outside or through a sunny window.” Goal Zero panels have never failed her, “and they’ll even work with some overcast, which is rare with the smaller solar panels.”

Survival Mom recommends having a solar light and prefers a collapsible one, “so it can be tucked into a backpack, glove box, or any other small area.”

If you’re worried about the possibility of a nuclear electromagnetic pulse event — the likes of which could potentially short-circuit your personal electronic equipment, and came up in conversation with many of the preppers we talked to — then James suggests investing in Faraday protection for your all-important phone and laptop.

entry.title: On My Mind: All the Ways I Retinol
entry.summary: Our beauty writer is slathering herself in face, neck, and body retinoids.
entry.content:
During the pandemic, I started consistently using prescription tretinoin. It faded my freckles, a benefit I hadn’t anticipated, but the persistent dryness and flaking led me to switch to an over-the-counter retinal, which helped maintain my results with less irritation. (I wrote about my experience with a retinal cream from K-beauty brand Celimax here.)

Now that I’m 46, fine lines and dark spots aren’t my biggest concerns; skin laxity is, particularly on my lower face and neck. I attended a launch event for Cottonball, a new customized prescription-skin-care brand back in September. The brand takes into account the products you already use, climate, sensitivity, skin type and tone, and health history to tailor tretinoin formula (it adds in other ingredients, such as hyaluronic acid, ceramides, bakuchiol, tranexamic acid, and niacinamide). Mine arrived as two prescriptions, one for my face and one for my neck, with a lower concentration of tretinoin in the latter.

So far, the adjustment has been surprisingly easy: I’ve experienced a little flaking on my neck, almost none on my face, and no significant irritation or initial breakout (often called a purge). My skin already looks smooth and brighter, but it’s too early to judge longer-term firming results. For now, I’m sticking with it.

I’m also looking beyond my face. As I’ve noticed more cellulite on my thighs, I’m wondering whether thinning body skin might be making the dimpling more apparent. Because retinoids are among the few topical ingredients with evidence of stimulating collagen production, body-retinol creams have caught my attention, too.

Dermatologist Kavita Mariwalla, MD, explained that results on the body may take much longer than on the face because body skin is thicker. Still, I’m willing to give them a shot.

I’ve been using Nécessaire’s Body Retinol nightly, and I love how smooth it leaves my skin. It’s also fragrance-free, a major plus for me since fragranced body products sometimes trigger hives. I haven’t experienced any irritation or flaking.

This one pairs retinol with ceramides and a copper peptide for additional firming benefits. It’s really lightweight and absorbs quickly.

I’ve always loved Josie Maran’s body butters. The consistencies are so good and leave my skin so smooth and well moisturized. This one has retinol derived from lab-grown algae and also contains the brand’s signature argan oil.

Working at the Strategist has made me realize I’m just not fussy enough about my bedding. I get decent sleep, but my sheets are basic, my pillows are nothing special, and my comforter could use an upgrade. I’ll start with some new sheets — higher thread count and a soft, buttery sateen finish.

I’ve also been basic with Advent calendars over the years. Our elf has always bought the old-school cardboard calendars with the chocolates on December 1. But our Advent-calendar roundups at the Strategist have me tempted to step it up this year with more fun calendars. My teens would love this one from Anthropologie that contains mini-size beauty products, including Mario Badescu Facial Spray and L’Occitane Almond Shower Oil.

And for my my 9-year-old, I love this fun Advent calendar with hair accessories. She’s very into wearing clips and scrunchies and trying different hairstyles lately.

I need new jeans and spotted these in the Strategist Readers’ Choice Award winners story. They are dressed up enough for work.
